Arlington, Massachusetts · The Call–Bartlett House

216 Pleasant Street: A Complete History

One Greek Revival house above Spy Pond, and the households that have filled it, as far as the records reach — an ice dealer's speculation, an art school principal's forty years, a grocer whose wife received letters from Helen Keller, the grocer's own family breaking up the estate, a 27-year tenure the directories never named, and an MIT scholar — from 1854 to the present owners.

How to read the labels

Every claim in this history carries the confidence the records support:

Confirmed stated in a primary record, or in two independent reliable sources.

Inference reasoned from cited evidence, not directly stated.

Unproven asserted by one secondary source or by tradition, not yet tested.

Not found searched for, and not located in the sources available online — with the exact record that would settle it named.

The deed chain from 1954 to the present is closed from the registry itself: the Hunter family subdivided the estate in 1954–56, Helen S. Brine held the house for 27 years, and the Russells bought from her in 1981. In November 2026 the previous owner, Rob Russell, passed along his own research on the estate — four pages of typed notes with handwritten additions, compiled from deeds and Arlington resident lists, and received second-hand by the current owners. They are transcribed in full, with photographs of the pages, in The Russell Notes below, and flagged wherever this history relies on them alone. The notes document the Bartlett estate's 1923 sale of the house lot to Henry H. Hunter, and name people the web research never found — an 1854 buyer recorded as "Henry E. Cole," an occupant E. W. Corey in 1875 — a placement since confirmed from a primary source by the 1875 Beers Atlas plate (see the Beers note below) — and John H. Hubbell, who sold the estate to Bartlett in 1886 — so they complicate the current owners' six-owner count at its first link while confirming it everywhere else. What is still open is stated plainly where it occurs. Chapter 7 tests the chain link by link; the final reference section lists every open question with the record that would settle it.

Research log — the November 2026 verification notes, in full

Bartlett completion pass + Hunter vital-records pass — November 21–22, 2026. A further hard-evidence pass worked the Bartlett family and the Hunter vital records item by item. Its main positive results are folded in throughout: Julia Bartlett's marriage was then narrowed to two GRO candidates — Sherriff (Bermondsey, June 1862, 1d 103) and Clark (Barnet, December 1866, 3a 185) — a result since displaced by a Dec 1857 Newington entry (George Hartnell Bartlett / Julia Louisa Smith, 1d 347), a strong index-grade candidate for the marriage and for the maiden name Smith (see the marriage note immediately below); Sharon Stanton Russell's dissertation is identified — Uneasy welcome — the political economy in migration policy in Kuwait, MIT PhD 1987 under Myron Weiner (MIT DSpace, no abstract carried); Carita B. Hunter is identified as Carita Hunter Lovejoy (Simmons '19, Mrs. Victor C. Lovejoy of Melrose by 1927, Tufts instructor in Shorthand and Typewriting from 1929); a candidate household member, Edward H. H. Bartlett, appears at 216 in the 1909 poll list (relationship unproven); and the MacJannet Vacation School of French is confirmed by Tufts' own biography as established in 1944 and “Located in Arlington, MA” — with no street address in any Tufts source read; the MacJannets' residence is since settled at 208 by the 1950 census margin (see the November 21, 2026 note below), so a school at 216 or 218 is unproven / unsupported. Everything else that pass searched for — Julia's death (searched 1923–1935; her death-or-removal window has since been narrowed to April 1924–April 1925 by the True Lists of 1924 and 1925 — see the 1924–25 note below), the Globe obituary, the “Po…” child, Ethel's death, Helen S. Brine, Barry Hunter's birth, Geraldine's marriage, Harry's and Florence's deaths, Thomas Forest, and Mary K. Dunleavy after 1926 — returned no hard record from open indexes, and each is marked Not found below with its search coverage and the archive record that would settle it. Massachusetts vital indexes for most of those sit in paywalled or archive-only collections (Ancestry / NEHGS / Massachusetts Archives) that could not be read signed-out.

George and Julia Bartlett's marriage — a strong index-grade candidate found, November 2026. A live FreeBMD search of GRO marriages (Bartlett, George, spouse first name Julia, 1855–1863) returned exactly two matches, the first being: Marriages Dec 1857 — Bartlett, George Hartnell, Newington, volume 1d, page 347. The four entries on that index page are George Hartnell Bartlett, Ann Harvey, Elias Morton, and Julia Louisa Smith — the page's only Julia. George's full Hartnell name, the bride's names matching his wife Julia Louisa (Julia L.), the Dec 1857 date fitting the marriage of about 1858 that both the 1900 census (married 42 years) and the 1910 census (married 52 years) report, and Newington's location in South London adjoining Camberwell make this a very strong candidate for the couple's marriage, and for Julia's maiden name being Smith.Unproven — strong index-grade candidate, not Confirmed The other couple on the page (Elias Morton / Ann Harvey) means the index alone does not prove the pairing — a GRO index page does not state which groom married which bride. The GRO marriage certificate for Dec 1857, Newington, vol. 1d, p. 347 is the settling record and has not yet been obtained. This 1857 entry displaces the two later candidates carried until now — Sherriff (Bermondsey, June 1862, 1d 103) and Clark (Barnet, December 1866, 3a 185) — which post-date the censuses' marriage date and whose groom entries carry “George” alone, without the Hartnell name. See Chapter 2, “The marriage,” and ledger Item 30.

Hard-evidence verification — November 22, 2026. A verification pass read the records themselves, rather than any second-hand chronology, and its results are folded in throughout and summarized in the verification ledger. Decisive: the Arlington True Lists were read in the books themselves (Internet Archive) — the Hunter household is at 216 Pleasant in every list read, 1928 through January 1, 1950, and is gone entirely by January 1, 1951; the second-hand claim that a Geraldine M. Hunter appears at 216 in 1951 is refuted by the 1951 book itself. Thomas Forest is at 216 in 1928 and 1933 and absent in 1936, exactly as claimed. The Massachusetts Historical Commission's Form B (No. 376) names the original owner Henry Call (not Cole) and dates the house 1855. Not settled: no draft card was found under either "Henry H." or "Harry H." Hunter, so the legal-name claim is untested — every Arlington record read names him Harry H. Hunter; no Massachusetts death-index entry for Agatha Hunter could be retrieved, so only list-based brackets stand; and the 1930/1940 census pages, the 1950 margin address, the PastPerfect photo record, and the MassLandRecords index could not be read in that pass, each with its locator named; the 1950 margin address has since been settled by the follow-up read below.

True Lists 1952–1954 — follow-up read, November 2026. The next three books were then read from the Archive.org page images (printed pp. 79, 79, and 78; PDFs archived in the project archive). Harry H. Hunter and Geraldine Hunter are at 216 in all three years:Confirmed 1952 — Harry H. Hunter, 65, grocer; M. Geraldine Hunter, 54, housewife, her 1951 residence given as Philadelphia. 1953 — H. H. Hunter, 66, retired; M. Geraldine Hunter, 51, at home. 1954 — Harry H. Hunter, 67, retired; Geraldine M. Hunter, 51, housewife. Russell's notes are therefore confirmed for 1952 and 1953 and refuted only for 1951; Geraldine's residence at 216 is established for 1952–54, and she had come from Philadelphia. Her listed ages — 54, then 51, then 51 — are inconsistent, so her birth year stays unsettled. The same pages fix the neighbors: 218 held the Marshalls in 1952, had no listed residents in 1953, and held Robert H. and Patricia White, newly from California, in 1954; the MacJannets were still at 208 in 1953 (age and occupation shown as dashes) and gone by 1954.

True Lists 1955–1957 — follow-up read, November 2026. The next three books were then read from the Archive.org page images (1955 printed p. 79, 1956 printed p. 78, 1957 printed p. 79; archived in the project archive), and they close the Hunter era and open the Brine one.Confirmed Harry H. and Geraldine Hunter, at 216 on January 1, 1954, are gone by January 1, 1955 and appear nowhere in the 1955, 1956, or 1957 lists — they left during calendar 1954, the year Helen S. Brine took the Lot B deed (June 30, 1954). At 216 on January 1, 1955 stand six people, every one with their 1954 residence given as Somerville: Frances S. Brine (89, retired), Helen S. Brine (64, personnel), Frances M. Frost (69, teacher), Frank H. Scammell (22, student), Henry Scammell (21, investigator), and Madeline B. Scammell (56, teacher). The same six are at 216 on January 1, 1956. On January 1, 1957 only four remain — Helen S. Brine (66, retired), Frances M. Frost (71), Frank H. Scammell (24, engineer), and Madeleine Scammell (58, teacher); Frances S. Brine and Henry Scammell are gone. The lists give no relationships among the six, and none is stated here. At 218 the same books show the Whites in 1955, then Robert M. and Leona Weiss Brownell, newly from Virginia, in 1956–57. Two things stay open:Unproven / open where Harry and Geraldine Hunter went after 1954 (a deed shows Harry alive on February 14, 1956), and whether Frances S. Brine died in 1956.

1875 Beers Atlas — plate read, November 2026. F. W. Beers, County Atlas of Middlesex, Massachusetts (1875), Arlington village plate, printed pp. 103–104 (with the town plate p. 101), was read from the Archive.org page images and archived in the project archive (maps-plans).Confirmed The plate letters the pond side of Pleasant Street, north to south, as held by Hodgdon, Mrs. A. Gage, Capt. R. Hopkins, P. H. Peabody, S. B. Hinks, A. Griffith & Hewes, J. T. Trowbridge, Chas. Hill, C. W. Chamberlin, T. C. Bucknam, J. C. Weld, E. Gould, M. Morton, Chas. O. Gage, and E. W. Corey — whose lot ran from Pleasant Street to the Spy Pond shore and carried two buildings, one at the street and one mid-lot on a dashed drive — then Mrs. M. Payson / First Cong. Society / N. Pratt Est., Mrs. Mayo, and G. Hill. This confirms, from a primary source, that E. W. Corey held a pond-side Pleasant Street parcel in the 216 stretch in 1875; the earlier “E. W. Corey” lead from Russell's notes is now plate-confirmed. That the Corey lot is exactly today's 216 Pleasant Street is labelled Inference — house numbering and the 1954–56 Hunter subdivision intervened, and only the deeds settle the lot equivalence; the mid-lot building position is consistent with the house's set-back, elevated siting. As an observation, not a conclusion: the lot immediately south of Corey's was lettered “Mrs. M. Payson” — a Payson holding beside the Corey/Call parcel — while the Call family's own history includes an Emily Payson Call connection; no kinship is shown on the plate. See Chapter 1, Chapter 6, and ledger Item 15.

1950 Census — MacJannet margin read, November 21, 2026. The 1950 U.S. Census page for Arlington ED 9-38 (sheet 4, NARA image 5 of 34) was read from the NARA page image and cross-checked on the FamilySearch image of the same page (ark:/61903/3:1:3QHN-PQHW-R99Q-C), and it settles Donald MacJannet's address.Confirmed His dwelling 33 margin address is 208 Pleasant Street — not 216 and not 218. The margin sequence on that page is 224 (Far), 220 (Gray), 216 (Harry H. Hunter, dwelling 32, line 10), 208 (MacJannet, dwelling 33, lines 11–15), 200 (Powers); there is no 218 on this page. The MacJannet household at 208: Donald MacJannet, 56, college administrator; his wife Chanette B., 48, born Germany, eurythmics teacher; lodgers Mrs. Frank V. Noyes, 74, widowed, and Maude Patten, 57, executive secretary; and nephew Klaus Blensdorf, 20, born Germany. This confirms the 1949–1951 Arlington True Lists placing the MacJannets at 208. Any claim that MacJannet's Vacation School of French was at 216 or 218 is Unproven — unsupported by the census and the town lists. Citations: NARA 1950 Census ED 9-38 search and the FamilySearch image above, logged in the project archive manifest (citation-only entry; image download was blocked by a login page). See Chapter 3 and ledger Item 16.

1940 Census and the “Bartlett Homestead” photograph — two primary sources read, November 2026. Confirmed The 1940 U.S. Census page for Arlington ED 9-26, Sheet 11A (NARA Catalog NAID 126377073, T627 Roll 1601, enumerated April 22, 1940; image archived in the project archive as census/1940-ed9-26-sheet11a.jpg) shows at 216 Pleasant Street: Harry H. Hunter, 53, head, home owned valued at $11,000, manager of a retail grocery; his wife Agatha F. B. Hunter, 51, born Canada-English; and their daughter Joan Hunter, 16, born in Massachusetts, highest grade completed H-2 (Sheet 11A, line 38) — a daughter not previously documented on this page. A re-read of the archived page image (November 22, 2026) shows the enumerator wrote “Joan”; the “Jean” carried in earlier versions of this history was a misreading of the handwriting. At 218 Pleasant Street: Florence V. Hunter, 79, widowed, living alone, home owned valued at $9,000, born Canada-English, same house in 1935. No Thomas Forest and no Mary K. Dunleavy appears at either address in 1940. Harry's 1939 wage entry is smudged and illegible in the census image, so no wage figure is stated. Confirmed The Arlington Historical Society PastPerfect record 2007.1.52 has also been read: the record is titled “Big Book p.52” (1920–1942, 8 images), and its image 8 is captioned “Bartlett Homestead, 216 Pleasant St” and shows the house from the street — white two-story clapboard, two chimneys, trees, a utility pole, and a 1940s car in front. The image is CC BY-NC-ND, with rights status not evaluated. See Chapter 2, Chapter 3, and ledger Items 17–18.

Joan Hunter — the name corrected, and her senior yearbook entry read, November 22, 2026. The Hunter daughter is Joan Hunter, not Jean.Confirmed Two primary records settle it. (1) The 1940 census page image (ED 9-26, Sheet 11A, line 38), re-read November 22, 2026: the enumerator wrote “Joan” — Harry and Agatha Hunter's daughter, 16, born in Massachusetts, highest grade completed H-2; the earlier “Jean” was a misreading of the handwriting. (2) The Arlington High School yearbook, Class of 1941, printed p. 41, carries her senior entry, with her portrait: “JOAN HUNTER, 216 Pleasant Street, Ski Club, Riding Club — Interesting Joan agrees that there is nothing like sailing. She'll never forget her Fine Arts class… Jackson is the college for her.” Her name, her Arlington High School class of 1941, and her intention to attend Jackson College are Confirmed. A third primary record now settles the next step: the Tufts Jumbo yearbook of 1942, student directory, “Class of 1945—Jackson” section (printed p. 181), lists “JOAN HUNTER, Alpha Xi Delta — 216 Pleasant Street, Arlington, Mass.” — her attendance at Jackson College (Tufts) is Confirmed. She did not receive a Jackson College degree: every Tufts degree ceremony from October 22, 1944 through June 15, 1947 has now been read from the Commencement Office's own programs — including the previously missing Degree Convocation of October 21, 1945 — and she appears in none of them (see the commencement note immediately below and ledger Item 25) Confirmed. She left Tufts without graduating Confirmed. Her birth record, her marriage, and her later life remain Not found — still being researched, and no later-life details are stated anywhere in this history. See Chapter 3 and ledger Items 23–25.

Joan Hunter — no Jackson College degree: every ceremony from October 1944 through June 1947 now read, including the fall-1945 convocation (verified negative), November 2026. Joan Hunter did not receive a Jackson College degree.Confirmed Every Tufts degree ceremony from October 22, 1944 through June 15, 1947 has now been read from the Commencement Office's own programs, and Joan Hunter appears in none of them. The Jackson College candidate lists were read in full in the official programs for the Degree Convocation of October 22, 1944, the Degree Convocation of February 18, 1945, and the 89th Annual Commencement of June 17, 1945 — all three programs archived in the project archive from the Tufts Digital Library. The one ceremony previously missing has now also been read: the Degree Convocation of October 21, 1945 (Tufts Digital Library record jq086051m), whose Jackson College lists — BA: Bedworth, Bowles, Fitzpatrick, Gaffny, Hogan, Hunt, Lane; BS: Fowler; BS in Chemistry: Carter, Hawes — contain no Hunter. The Tufts Ninety-first Annual Commencement program of June 15, 1947 (Tufts Digital Library, archived) has likewise been read from the page image: Joan Hunter appears in none of its Jackson College degree lists, and its “degrees awarded subsequent” section names only two dental graduates. With every ceremony in the span read, the negative is complete: she took no Jackson degree Confirmed, and she left Tufts without graduating Confirmed. Her birth record, her marriage, and her later life remain Not found — still being researched. See Chapter 3 and ledger Item 25.

1912 Homer manuscript and the 218 MACRIS record — two sources read, November 2026. Mrs. Horace H. Homer's Pleasant Street — Ancient and Modern (1912, Arlington Historical Society manuscript; typewritten copy 1985.33.15), under the heading “BARTLETT.” on printed p. 32, gives the ownership chain before Bartlett:Unproven — manuscript statement, not deed-proven Henry Call purchased the estate in 1854 from Mr. Hill, built the house, lived there a few years, then sold to Mr. Charles Burchard, who sold to Mr. Corey, from whom Prof. George Bartlett purchased it — so on this account Bartlett bought from Corey, not directly from Call. The conflicts stand unresolved: an earlier lead had Call buying from Addison Gage in 1854 (the manuscript says Hill — Unproven either way until the 1854 deed is read), and another had Bartlett buying from John H. Hubbell in 1886 (contradicted by the manuscript, still Unproven). The National Register form cited this manuscript at “p. 26,” but in the typewritten copy the Bartlett passage is on printed p. 32 (p. 26 covers Peabody/Hicks) — the page-citation mismatch is flagged, not resolved. Separately, MACRIS record ARL.1244 names 218 Pleasant Street “Call, Henry Barn” — the state's inventory itself calls it Henry Call's barn Confirmed at inventory level — but the record carries no inventory form and no construction date, so whether the barn was built before, with, or after the 1854/55 house remains Unproven pending the assessor field card (see the November 21, 2026 note below and ledger Item 22). See Chapter 1, the Prologue's estate section, and ledger Items 19–20.

1850 Census — the entire West Cambridge schedule now read, and Henry Call is not in it, November 2026. The entire 1850 U.S. Census schedule for West Cambridge (now Arlington), Middlesex County, Massachusetts — NARA microfilm reel M432-324, families 1–402, every page read from the page images — has now been read in full.Confirmed — from the record itself It contains no Henry Call, no Henry E. Cole, no Burchard, no Corey, and no Gage. Henry Call was therefore not living in West Cambridge in 1850, four years before he bought the estate in 1854; the earlier report that he was “formerly of Charlestown” remains the live lead for where he came from. Charles Burchard (who, per the 1912 Homer manuscript, bought the house from Call) and Sarah Ann Burchard likewise do not appear in West Cambridge in 1850, and neither does E. W. Corey, who held the lot by 1875. The Hills, however, are there in force — written page 332 (image n320, archived) shows a Hill cluster in consecutive households: Amos Hill, 76, with $8,000 in real estate; Amos Hill Jr., 40, farmer, $12,500; and Henry W. Hill, 38, farmer, $12,800 Confirmed census facts — neighboring farmers with $8,000–$12,800 in real estate, the candidate pool for the “Mr. Hill” the Homer manuscript names as Call's 1854 seller. Which Hill sold is still Unproven — no record yet says which Hill sold. See Chapter 1 and ledger Items 12 and 26.

Nomination photograph and the MACRIS records — verification run, November 21, 2026. Two further records were read in full and archived. Confirmed The National Register nomination file for the Call–Bartlett House (NRIS 85001024, NPS NPGallery) contains exactly one photograph: a front (Pleasant Street) elevation. That photograph is the same frame as the front-elevation black-and-white print in the house file — identical trees, overhead wire, chimney, and window curtains; the nomination copy is cropped tighter. The back of that print, also in the house file, is handwritten “Call-Bartlett House, 216 Pleasant St., Arlington MRA” with no photographer credit. The other nine black-and-white prints in the house file (interiors, pond-side porch, covered porch) do not appear in the nomination file — so the print set as a whole is not the nomination photo set; only the front-elevation print is the nomination photograph. The set's overall date and photographer remain Unproven. Confirmed — as a negative The Massachusetts Historical Commission inventory record for 216 (MACRIS ARL.447, Form B No. 376) was also read in full, including both MACRIS PDFs: it lists “Outbuildings: None,” gives the construction date as 1855 only, and makes no mention of a barn, a carriage house, or 218 Pleasant Street. The MACRIS page shows no individual National Register number for the house — only the designation dates (National Register 04/18/1985; Local Historic District 09/13/1991); the NRIS number 85001024 comes from NPS records. For 218 Pleasant (MACRIS ARL.1244, “Call, Henry Barn”), MACRIS still gives no construction date — that date remains Unproven pending the assessor field card. See the Prologue's estate section, the Plates table, and ledger Items 21–22.

1869–70 Directory — Charles Birchard on Pleasant Street, and no Call or Corey in Arlington, November 2026. The Somerville, Arlington and Belmont Directory for 1869–70 (Dudley & Greenough, 1869; Archive.org item arlingtoncitydir1869arli; page images archived in the project archive) has been read from its own pages.Confirmed P. 162 lists “Birchard Charles, wholesale grocer (183 State, B.), house Pleasant, near Spy Pond” — the spelling is BIRCHARD, not the “Burchard” used in the 1912 Homer manuscript — and p. 168 lists “Donnelly Patrick, gardener, Charles Birchard's, Pleasant,” so Birchard kept an estate with a resident gardener on Pleasant Street in 1869. The same directory confirms the pond-side neighbours: p. 170 “Gage Anna, widow Addison, house Pleasant, n. Spy Pond” (Addison Gage was dead by 1869) and “Gage Charles O. ice dealer (128 State, B.), house Pleasant, near Spy Pond”; p. 176 “Libby Jackson H. foreman of ice business for Addison, Gage & Co.”; and pp. 172–173 Charles Hill, George Hill, and Mary Hill all living on Pleasant near the pond. Not found — verified negative The directory's Arlington C-section (pp. 164–166) was read in full: it contains no Corey or Cory entry and no Call entry — neither E. W. Corey nor Henry Call was an Arlington resident in 1869, consistent with the Homer manuscript chain (Call sold to Birchard, who sold to Corey, who sold to Bartlett), with Corey appearing as the lot's owner only by the 1875 Beers atlas. That Birchard's Pleasant Street house was the Call house (today's 216) is Inference — the directory gives no house numbers, so the equivalence is not proven by the directory itself. Unproven Sarah Ann Burchard (of the 1857 Gage lease in Rob Russell's notes) may be recorded under the spelling “Birchard”; searches under both spellings have so far found no matching person, and her identity remains open. See Chapter 1, Chapter 6, and ledger Item 27.

1871–72 Directory — E. W. Corey identified as E. Willis Corey, and Birchard gone, November 2026. The Arlington Directory for 1871 & 2 (Greenough, Jones & Co., Boston, 1871; Archive.org item arlingtoncitydir1871arli), printed p. 195, lists: “Corey E. Willis, leather, (223 Congress, B.), h. Pleasant” — the E. W. Corey who held the 216 Pleasant Street lot in the 1875 Beers Atlas is therefore E. Willis Corey, a Boston leather dealer at 223 Congress Street whose house was on Pleasant Street in Arlington.Confirmed The directory gives no more of his name: what the initial “E.” stands for is not stated, and expanding “E. Willis” to a full first name remains Unproven. The same directory's Arlington B section (printed pp. 192–194), read in full, contains no entry at all for Charles Birchard — the wholesale grocer listed at Pleasant near Spy Pond in the 1869–70 directory, spelled Birchard there — so the Birchard-to-Corey transition on Pleasant Street falls between the 1869–70 and 1871–72 directories.Confirmed See Chapter 6 and ledger Item 28.

1930 Census read, and the Corey probate index — November 22, 2026. Two more primary records have been read and folded in. Confirmed The 1930 U.S. Census page for the estate (ED 9-169, Sheet 10B, NARA T626 roll 914, enumerated April 12, 1930) shows at 216: Harry H. Hunter (43, home owned valued at $10,000 as first written, overwritten to read $60,000 (disputed reading — the value digit is heavily overwritten), radio set, manager of a groceries company), his wife Agatha (40), daughter Joan (6, in school), Agatha's father Thomas Forrest (79 — entered as Harry's father-in-law, which settles the Forest relationship), and servant Mary Dunleavy (34, born in the Irish Free State); at 218, Florence V. Hunter (69) rents at $75 a month, with a radio set; and no household at 212 or 214 appears on the sheet. Ledger Item 3 is closed; see Chapter 3, “The 1930 census.” Confirmed The Index to the Probate Records of Suffolk County, Vol. 1, printed p. 239, lists “1891 — Corey, E. Willis — will — No. 86371”: Elijah Willis Corey left a will probated in Suffolk County in 1891, confirming he had died by 1891; the exact death date and the will file's contents remain Unproven / not yet read. See Chapter 1.

1900 Directory — the Bartlett house becomes 216 Pleasant, and the renumbering is shown, November 2026. The Arlington and Belmont Directory for 1900 (Edward A. Jones, copyright 1900; Archive.org item arlingtoncitydir1900arli; page images archived in the project archive) has been read from its own pages.Confirmed Printed p. 22 lists “George H. Prof., principal Normal Art school (studio 27 Tremont, B.), h. 216 Pleasant,” with Edward H. Bartlett, Ernest S. Bartlett (clerk), Ethel G. Bartlett (art teacher), and Julia L. Bartlett (Miss) all boarding at 216 Pleasant; the book's Pleasant Street list (printed p. 172) repeats 216 for Prof. & Mrs. George H. Bartlett, Edward H. Bartlett, and Miss Julia L. Bartlett, between 208 (Freeman N. Young; Frank E. Thompson) and 226 (Samuel G. Prentiss). This is the first record found that gives the Bartlett house its modern number, 216 Pleasant: Pleasant Street was renumbered between the 1894 directory (the Bartletts at 88 Pleasant) and 1900, and the same household — with the same Prentiss neighbor beside it (92 in 1894, 226 in 1900) — appears at both numbers, so the 88 = 216 equivalence is now shown by the directories themselves.Confirmed The directory's Arlington C section was read in full: no Corey or Cory appears in it — the book's only Corey entry is in its Belmont section, a different town — extending E. Willis Corey's Arlington absence in directories to 1883–1900.Confirmed That Julia L. (Miss) is George's daughter Julia Lavinia is Inference — the directory does not state the relationship. See Chapter 2, Chapter 6, and ledger Item 29.

1900 Census — the Bartlett household at 216 Pleasant, read, November 2026. The 1900 U.S. Census page for the house (ED 658, Sheet 1B, NARA T623 roll 655, enumerated June 1, 1900; page image archived in the project archive) has been read from the page image.Confirmed At 216 Pleasant — dwelling 18, family 19 — stand George H. Bartlett (entered as b. May 1835, England; immigrated 1866; naturalized; Teacher of Art; the home owned, with a mortgage), his wife Julia L. Bartlett (b. July 1839, England; married 42 years; immigrated 1870), and the census's own figures for Julia: 13 children born, 9 living. Edward H. H. Bartlett is entered explicitly as George's son (b. July 1861, England; immigrated 1872) — the relationship the 1909 poll list left unstated is now resolved, and he is the eldest known Bartlett child. Also in the household: daughter Julia L. (b. Jan. 1866, artist in lithography), daughter Ethel G. (b. Aug. 1867, Teacher of Art), son Ernest S. (b. Oct. 1875, Massachusetts), son George S. F. (b. Sept. 1880, Massachusetts, at school) — a newly identified child — and a boarder, Annie E. Blake (b. Sept. 1845, Massachusetts; Teacher of Art). The census records the family's immigration years as staggered — George 1866, Julia 1870, Edward 1872, the daughters 1874 — and they are reported here as recorded, without explanation. The census's “married 42 years” (c. 1857–58) now fits the strong index-grade candidate found since — the Dec 1857 Newington GRO entry (George Hartnell Bartlett / Julia Louisa Smith, 1d 347) — and Edward's July 1861 birth follows that marriage; Julia's maiden name Smith is therefore a strong candidate, not yet proven, the Newington certificate not yet obtained.Unproven — strong index-grade candidate, not Confirmed See Chapter 2 and ledger Item 30.

Cambridge Directory for 1872 — Corey gone from Cambridge, November 2026. The Cambridge Directory for 1872 (printed p. 100; page image archived in the project archive) no longer lists Elijah Willis Corey in Cambridge — the book's only Corey is an unrelated Amelia Corey.Confirmed The absence is consistent with his move to Arlington by 1870, where the 1870 census already places him. See Chapter 1 and ledger Item 31.

Boston directories 1880–1886 and the Dorchester Blue Book 1885 — Corey after Arlington, November 2026. The Boston city directories for 1880–1886 and the Dorchester Blue Book for 1885 (all read from page images and archived in the project archive) now trace Elijah Willis Corey after he left Arlington.Confirmed 1880 — partner in Corey & Bond, horse equipments, 234/236 Purchase Street, Boston; living at the Waverley House in Charlestown. 1881–1883 — dealing in hides and leather (140 Pearl, then 224 Congress, then 34 High), living at the Hotel Falmouth. 1884 — his trade has changed to games and novelties at 133 Pearl; still at the Hotel Falmouth. 1885 — business still at 133 Pearl, but his house is now 8 Batchelder Street, Dorchester; the 1885 Dorchester Blue Book lists him there under his full name, “Elijah Willis Corey.” 1886 — listed at 8 Batchelder with no business address printed. Where he and his family were enumerated in the 1880 census remains Unproven — a Charlestown hotel household is the lead. See Chapter 1 and ledger Item 32.

Boston Directory for 1887 — Corey & Andrews, and Willis C. Corey reappears, November 2026. The Boston Directory for 1887 (printed p. 289) lists “Corey E. Willis (Corey & Andrews), 86 Bedford, h. 8 Batchelder” — the firm Corey & Andrews sold boot and shoe machinery at 86 Bedford Street, Boston, and Elijah Willis Corey still lived at 8 Batchelder Street, Dorchester.Confirmed The same page lists his son: “Corey Willis C. messenger, Blackstone Nat. Bank, bds. 8 Batchelder” — Willis C. Corey (born about 1867, the young child in the 1870 Arlington census household) was a messenger at the Blackstone National Bank boarding at his father's house.Confirmed This is Willis C.'s first appearance in a record since 1870. See Chapter 1 and ledger Item 33.

Annie E. Blake identified — Massachusetts Normal Art School catalogue, 1899–1900, November 2026. The boarder Annie E. Blake in the 1900 census household at 216 Pleasant (born Sept. 1845, Massachusetts, Teacher of Art) is identified by the Massachusetts Normal Art School catalogue for 1899–1900, whose Instructors page lists, under Principal George H. Bartlett, “ANNIE E. BLAKE — Modelling and Casting; Design in the Round.”Confirmed She was Bartlett's faculty colleague at the school in the year she boarded at 216 — a colleague living with the principal. Her birth and death records and her later life remain Not found. See Chapter 2 and ledger Item 34.

Boston Directories for 1889 and 1890 — Corey's run extended to 1890, November 2026. Elijah Willis Corey's Boston-directory run does not end in 1887. The Boston Directory for 1889 lists “Corey E. Willis, supt. h. 8 Batchelder, Dor.” and the directory for 1890 lists him again at the same address and in the same role (page images archived in the project archive).Confirmed His absence from the 1888 directory was a one-year omission, not his death or departure. His son Willis C. Corey (messenger, Blackstone National Bank) boards at 8 Batchelder in both years, and a Chester Corey (clerk) also boards there in 1889 and 1890 — his relationship is unstated, so he is labelled an Inference / Unproven household member, not a proven son. Corey's directory run now spans 1880–1890 with only the 1888 gap; his death and later endpoint remain Unproven / Not found. See Chapter 1 and ledger Item 35.

Boston Directory for 1896 — Corey's widow still at 21 Sargent Street, November 2026. Elijah Willis Corey's widow's household was still at 21 Sargent Street, Dorchester, in the 1896 Boston directory: Mrs. E. Willis Corey is the householder there, with Chester Corey, salesman, and Willis C. Corey, clerk at the Blackstone National Bank, boarding there.Confirmed Her tenure at that address now runs 1892–1896 in directory evidence. Elijah Willis Corey's own death record remains Not found — the widow listing shows he had died by 1896, but no death date or place is stated here. See Chapter 1 and ledger Item 38.

George Bartlett's Atlantic crossing — the Tripoli candidate tested and rejected, November 2026. The passenger-index candidate “George Bartlett, 26, arrived 1866, ship Tripoli” has now been tested against the manifest page itself — NARA microfilm M237, roll 268, S.S. Tripoli, Liverpool & Queenstown to New York, list sworn July 30, 1866 (page archived in the project archive) — and it is rejected: the manifest's George Bartlett is a 26-year-old English laborer travelling in a five-person party — Edmund Bartlett (63), Jane Bartlett (62, wife), George (26, laborer), Elizabeth Bartlett (25, wife), and Jane Bartlett (1, infant).Confirmed — from the manifest page itself That party, occupation, and age conflict with George H. Bartlett of 216 Pleasant — wife Julia Louisa; eldest child Edward born in England in 1861; art teacher; born 1835 per the 1900 census — so the Tripoli record is a tested-and-rejected same-name record, not his crossing. George's own Atlantic crossing remains Not found. The daughters' 1874 Boston arrival on the Siberia (index-grade) is unchanged. See Chapter 2 and ledger Item 36.

George Bartlett's Atlantic crossing — the second candidate, City of London (1870), also tested and rejected, November 2026. The second Castle Garden-era candidate has now been read at manifest level and is likewise rejected. The passenger manifest of the City of London (NARA M237 roll 330; master Henry Tibbits; from London; sworn at New York June 1, 1870) lists at entry 54 a Geo. Bartlett, age 29, occupation farmer, travelling alone in steerage from Great Britain.Confirmed — from the manifest itself That man is not George H. Bartlett: the 1900 census gives George's immigration year as 1866, his birth as May 1835, and his trade was art, not farming. With the Tripoli (1866) candidate also rejected at manifest level, George's own crossing remains Not found, as do Julia's (c. 1870) and Edward's (c. 1872); the daughters Julia and Ethel are identified at index level arriving at Boston in 1874 aboard the Siberia, with that manifest page still unread. See Chapter 2 and ledger Item 37.

One combined history — the Hunter family inside the house history. There is no separate Hunter-family space: the Hunter era is Chapter 3 of this single history of 216 Pleasant Street, with the family's people, deeds, subdivision, and later life carried in the chapters, timeline, Who's Who, and verification ledger below. All of the Helen Keller material is gathered together in Chapter 3 · II — The Helen Keller Letters: the 1923, 1932, and Thanksgiving letters, with photographs of the surviving pages and links to every auction listing, and every picture and document for the house — nomination, censuses, maps, yearbooks, deeds, and the Russell notes photographs — is linked in Plates & Documents.

1910 Census — the Bartlett household at 216 Pleasant, read, November 2026. Bartlett (71, Professor, Normal Art School), his wife Julia Bartlett (70; married 52 years; 13 children born, 9 living — unchanged from 1900), son Edward H. Bartlett (46), daughter Ethel G. Bartlett (42, Teacher, Art School), and boarder Annie E. Blake (65, Teacher, Art School). Julia L., Ernest S., and George S. F. Bartlett — all in the 1900 household — are absent. One conflict is flagged, not harmonized:Unproven / open the 1910 immigration years conflict with the 1900 census (George 1870 in 1910 vs 1866 in 1900; Julia 1871 vs 1870; Ethel 1873 vs 1874), while the two censuses' marriage durations — 42 years in 1900, 52 in 1910 — agree on a marriage of about 1858. See Chapter 2 and ledger Item 40.

Bartlett (81, born England, teacher at the Normal Art School; the home owned), his wife Julia (80, born England), and their daughter Ethel G. Blake — all present in earlier households at 216 — are not in the 1920 household.Confirmed Two conflicts are flagged, not harmonized:Inference / conflict the sheet writes a naturalization year of 1885 for all three, which conflicts with the October 24, 1887 naturalization date from other sources; and its immigration years (George 1870, Julia 1871, Ethel 1873) conflict with the 1900 and 1910 censuses. Boston Directories 1861–1870 — Birchard and the Gage ice family at West Cambridge, November 2026. The Boston Directory run for both families is now continuous 1861–1870 (page images read and archived).Confirmed In the 1861 directory (printed p. 49), Charles Birchard's entry reads “Birchard Charles (B. & Torrey), house at West Cambridge” and his firm “Birchard & Torrey (C. Birchard and J. M. Torrey), grocers, 183 State.” In the 1862 directory (printed p. 161), the Gage entries read “Gage Addison & Co. (C. O. Gage), ice, 70 State, house at West Cambridge” and “Gage Charles O. (A. Gage & Co.), ice, 70 State, h. at W. Cambridge.” One nuance is stated plainly: in 1861 Charles O. Gage's personal entry reads “h. at Charlestown” even though the firm's house is given as West Cambridge — he was still personally a Charlestown householder in 1861 and appears at West Cambridge from 1862. Whether Charles Birchard's West Cambridge house was this house (216 Pleasant) remains Inference, not Confirmed. See Chapter 1, Chapter 6, and ledger Item 49.

Streeter was listed separately, with a livery stable on Bromfield, and no cross-reference to Gage. Prologue

Overview

216 Pleasant Street stands on the south side of Pleasant Street (Massachusetts Route 60), its gable ends facing the street to the west and Spy Pond to the east — a house built to be looked at from the road and to look out at the water.

It is a Greek Revival, 2½-story, L-shaped wood-frame house with a cross-gabled roof, finished in flushboarding and clapboards.Confirmed The main (west) facade is three bays, the entrance in the left bay, framed by pilasters, a four-light transom, an entablature, and a gabled pediment. The pond-facing east facade carries the house's signature: a two-story Greek temple portico with four columns running the width of the house. The National Park Service's Arlington survey singles it out among the town's formal Greek Revival houses, "distinguished by extensive use of flush-board siding."

The house was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on April 18, 1985 (reference 85001024, Arlington Multiple Resource Area; Massachusetts Historical Commission Form B #376, recorded by Betsy Friedberg in January 1985), under Criteria B and C — for its architecture, and for its association with George Hartnell Bartlett. It also stands in the local Pleasant Street historic district. Today's lot is 0.27 acre (assessor parcel ARLI M:123.0 B:0002 L:0006.C, per aggregator records).

1854 or 1855?

The sources disagree with each other by a year, and the disagreement is in the record itself. The National Register nomination says 1855; the current owners' 2023 letter to the Zoning Board of Appeals and the body text of the house's Wikipedia article say 1854 — while that article's own lead paragraph says 1855. The MHC Form B itself (No. 376, recorded by Betsy Friedberg, MHC, January 1985) also says 1855, its style source given as the Menotomy Historic District Report.Confirmed as to what the form saysUnresolved The record that would settle it: Henry Call's land purchase in the Middlesex South Registry of Deeds grantor/grantee indexes (c. 1853–55), read against the 1854 and 1855 West Cambridge tax valuations, which would show the first year a house appears on the lot.

Alterations

The 1985 nomination records major alterations as "None" — then immediately hedges: "A possibility exists that this handsome residence was significantly altered in the third quarter of the 19th century by the introduction of a north wing and an expanded portico with chamfered posts."Confirmed, with the nomination's own caveat If so, the change likely dates to the Call-to-Bartlett transition. By 1985 the house still read as essentially unaltered Greek Revival — which also means the unknown owners of the mid-20th century were conservative stewards.

The estate

The original Call estate comprised today's 212, 214, 216, and 218 Pleasant Street; 218 was the carriage house and stables. The four parcels "remained connected by deed and/or family for the next 100 years until the early 1950s," in the current owners' words.Confirmed Number 216 retains a deeded easement giving it access to Spy Pond — stated in the owners' 2023 ZBA filing. Historically the lot had a direct pond view; the houses built on the subdivided pond-side parcels now stand between the house and the water. None of the four smaller houses on the pond side of the former estate — described in the nomination as one 18th-century, two 19th-century, and one recent — is part of the property today.

The state's own inventory ties 218 to Call by name. MACRIS record ARL.1244 names the property at 218 Pleasant Street “Call, Henry Barn” — the Massachusetts Historical Commission's inventory itself calls it Henry Call's barn.Confirmed at inventory level But the record stops there: it carries no inventory form and no construction date, so whether the barn was built before, with, or after the 1854/55 house remains Unproven — the date is still open pending the assessor field card. See ledger Items 20 and 22.

The inventory record for 216 itself is silent about the outbuildings altogether. MACRIS record ARL.447 (Form B No. 376), read in full in the November 21, 2026 verification run — including both MACRIS PDFs — lists “Outbuildings: None,” gives the construction date as 1855 only, and makes no mention of a barn, a carriage house, or 218 Pleasant Street.Confirmed — as a negative The MACRIS page likewise shows no individual National Register number for the house, giving only the designation dates — National Register 04/18/1985 and Local Historic District 09/13/1991; the NRIS number 85001024 cited throughout this history comes from NPS records, not from MACRIS. See ledger Item 22.

Reference

Residents by year

Every person the records place at 216 Pleasant Street, drawn as a Gantt chart — one row per resident, one column per year, from the house's building in 1854 to the present owners. Scroll the chart sideways to travel through the years and scroll it down through the households: the names column stays frozen on the left and the year row stays frozen at the top, so you never lose either axis. The corner where they meet stays put both ways.

Bars are drawn only where this history's evidence puts someone at 216. A solid bar means the run is confirmed in the deeds, censuses, directories, or the January 1 resident lists read for the chapters above; a hatched bar — or a hatched end to a bar — means the endpoint is bracketed between records, not proven to the year. The early decades are the softest: Call, Birchard, and Corey rest on the 1912 Homer manuscript, the directories, and the 1875 Beers plate, and Bartlett's arrival is bracketed in the 1880s before his 1886 purchase. Gaps inside a row are real gaps in the lists — Harry Hunter's missing 1951, Brooke Russell's 1997–2000 absence — not drawing errors. Residents of the carriage house at 218 are not charted here; the chart is 216 only.

Owner — confirmed run Household member — confirmed run Hatched — bracketed, not proven to the year

How the long runs read: Helen S. Brine, 1955–1981, is the longest single confirmed residence; Harry H. Hunter's household runs 1925–1954 with a one-year break in the 1951 list; Keith A. Larson, 1974–2004, is the bridge between houses — he arrives under Brine, stays on through the sale, and lives under the Russells for two more decades. The Russell era closes in the lists, which have now been read through 2018: Sharon Stanton Russell, present in every list from 1982 through 2012, no longer appears in 2013 — she died on February 27, 2013 — Robert Mitchell Russell remains at 216 through the 2014 list and is gone in 2015, ahead of the November 3, 2015 deed, and the Tarantellis are still carried at 216 in the January 1, 2016 list, where Matthew Dawson appears for the first time. That co-listing is a list artifact, not co-residence: the Dawsons confirm firsthand that they never overlapped with the Tarantellis — the Tarantellis were Russell-era occupants whose occupancy ended with the November 2015 sale — so their bars on the chart end in 2015, not 2016. In the January 1, 2017 list Matthew Dawson is the only resident listed at 216, and the Tarantellis no longer appear — a whole-book search finds no Tarantelli. In the January 1, 2018 list Matthew Dawson is again the only resident listed at 216, unchanged from 2017. Short-stay household members named in the lists for a single year or two — Doris C. Arnold (1931), Gladys MacLeod, Bertha J. Stephens, Nettie Richardson, Bessie Kobson (1941), Stella F. Horton (1944), Robert Roy (1947), Susanne Scammell (1959) — are transcribed year by year in The Russell Notes and in Chapters 3–4 rather than given rows of their own.

Cole, no Burchard, no Corey, and no Gage Confirmed — from the record itself — Henry Call was not living in West Cambridge in 1850, four years before he bought the estate in 1854; “formerly of Charlestown” remains the live lead. Charles and Sarah Ann Burchard likewise do not appear, and neither does E. W. Corey (who held the lot by 1875). Written p. 332 (image n320) shows the Hills in force — a Hill cluster in consecutive households: Amos Hill, 76, $8,000 in real estate; Amos Hill Jr., 40, farmer, $12,500; Henry W. Hill, 38, farmer, $12,800 Confirmed census facts — neighboring farmers with $8,000–$12,800 in real estate, the candidate pool for the “Mr. Hill” of the Homer manuscript (see 1854); which Hill sold is still Unproven.

Torrey), grocers, 183 State” Confirmed. The Boston Directory run for Birchard and for the Gage ice family is now continuous 1861–1870 Confirmed. In 1861 Charles O. Gage's personal entry reads “h. at Charlestown” even though the firm's house is given as West Cambridge — he was still personally a Charlestown householder in 1861. That Birchard's house was the Call house (today's 216) is Inference — the directory gives no house numbers. The same directory: Anna Gage, widow of Addison (dead by 1869), and Charles O. Gage, ice dealer, both on Pleasant near Spy Pond (p. 170); Jackson H. Libby, foreman of the ice business for Addison, Gage & Co. (p. 176); Charles, George, and Mary Hill on Pleasant near the pond (pp. 172–173). Its Arlington C-section (pp. 164–166, read in full) has no Corey or Cory and no Call Not found — verified negative — neither Corey nor Call was an Arlington resident in 1869, consistent with the Homer chain; Corey appears as the lot's holder only by the 1875 Beers atlas. Willis” to a full first name remains Unproven. Reference

Value

The chart shows the three headline figures documented for this house — two market sale prices and one insurance value — and the tables below it document every other value the records hold, each labelled by its type: deed transfers, nominal considerations, and census-reported values.Confirmed The 1854 purchase price and the other early considerations are not in the surviving online record, so the early years are a gap, not a guess: no figure is estimated for them.

Why the chart starts in 1981. The 1981 Brine-to-Russell deed is the earliest sale in the online address-search and assessor sales series used for this history — the digital sales record for this address reaches no further back, and the earlier transfers, from 1854 onward, sit in the registry's pre-digital books, whose stated considerations have not been read. The 1981 start is therefore a floor of the available series, not the beginning of the house's value history, and no pre-1981 sale price is stated or estimated anywhere on this page. Earlier figures do survive in different kinds of record — the owner-reported home values the censuses collected, and town assessed values from 1922–1926 — and they are tabulated separately below under their own labels: not drawn on the chart, and not mixed into the sale series. One earlier transfer is documented in the registry index — the Hunter family's June 30, 1954 deed of the house lot to Helen S. Brine (Bk 8280/600) — but the index states no consideration for it, so it appears in the table below as a transfer with no price, and nothing is filled in for it. Assessor valuation lists from the 1850s, which would give the house a contemporary assessed figure, are still being sought from the Robbins Library; until one is read, that series remains a stated gap.

They are listed here as their own series — in the nominal dollars of their own years, with the single-figure entries converted by the switch above — and none of them is a sale price or evidence of what the house would have sold for. The 1930 figure carries a warning of its own: the enumerator's value digit (Sheet 10B, line 58) is heavily overwritten, and the entry reads $10,000 as first written and $60,000 as finally written — both readings are published here, flagged, and neither is used alone.
