The other value types — what the record does and does not hold

Town assessed values. A run of assessed values for 216 is now verified Confirmed from the Assessors' Reports in the Town of Arlington Annual Reports, each read from the Archive.org page image and archived in the project archive, and each shown in the table above labelled as an assessed value, not a sale price. The 1922 report (printed p. 11) gives George H. Bartlett's property at 216 a total real assessed value of $8,725 — house $4,500, outbuilding $1,000, and 40,315 sq ft of land at $3,225, the components summing to the printed total — with a total tax of $279.20 and no personal property listed. The 1923 report (printed p. 23) assesses the same parcel to George H. Bartlett at $10,550 — house $5,500, outbuilding $1,000, land $4,050 — with a total tax of $279.58. The 1924 report (printed p. 110) assesses the parcel, at the same $10,550 and the same components, to Harry H. Hunter, assessed from his 181 Cedar Ave. address — so the assessors' own books bracket the Bartlett-to-Hunter ownership transfer between the 1923 and 1924 assessments (see Chapter 3). The 1925 report (printed p. 112), with Hunter now at 216, gives $20,050 — house $15,000, outbuilding $1,000, land $4,050; the house component rose from $5,500 to $15,000 between the 1924 and 1925 assessments, and the figures are recorded as printed. The 1926 report (printed p. 129) repeats the $20,050 total — house $15,000, the outbuilding now called “barn” at $1,000, land $4,050. One current assessed value is also verified Confirmed: the MassGIS Level 3 assessor extract of the Town of Arlington assessor database, FY2026 (archived in the project archive), gives this parcel (123.0-0002-0006.C) a total assessed value of $1,919,000 — building $1,026,700, land $892,300 — shown in the first table above, labelled as an assessed value (town assessor, FY2026): not a sale price and not a market estimate. The same record corroborates the 2015 sale — November 3, 2015, $1,000,000, Book 66331 Page 188. No other assessed value for 216 has been verified in the records read for this history. A figure of $1,417,000 for 2025 circulates in aggregator data, but it belongs to 218 Pleasant Street, not 216, and is not used here; for 218 itself, the same FY2026 extract gives an assessed total of $1,490,300, and its assessor year-built field prints 1850 — an assessor-database field only, Unproven as a construction date for the barn (see ledger Item 22). The assessor's field card for this parcel (123.0-0002-0006.C) has not been read, and the 1850s town valuation lists are not online — they are being sought at the Robbins Library. The only 1850s dollar figures anywhere in this history — the Hill households' total real-estate holdings in the 1850 census ($8,000–$12,800) — are a family's whole real-estate wealth, not a value for this parcel, and are not shown as values of the house.

Mortgage amounts. Mortgages on the property are documented as events — Henry Call's 1855 mortgage to Gage in Russell's notes, the Russells' trust-era refinancing in 2011 — but no amount for any of them is stated in the sources read, so no mortgage figure is shown.

Online estimates. No Zillow or Redfin estimate for 216 was retrieved in the November 2026 value sweep, so none is quoted. When one is captured it will be added here labelled as what it is — an automated estimate, with its source and access date — never as a sale price or an appraisal.

Probate inventories. The Bartlett, Corey, and Brine probate files, any of which may carry an inventoried value for the house or the estate, have not been read; Corey's Suffolk case (No. 86371, Chapter 1) is the named first pull.

Method. With the switch on, every figure above — table and chart alike — is converted to 2026 dollars with the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U), U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, series CUUR0000SA0 (U.S. city average, all items, not seasonally adjusted; BLS series page, read November 2026). Annual averages: 16.8 for 1922, 17.1 for 1923, 17.1 for 1924, 17.5 for 1925, 17.7 for 1926, 14.0 for 1940, 90.9 for 1981, and 237.017 for 2015. No 2026 annual average exists yet, so the 2026 reference point is the October 2026 monthly index, 337.511, the latest published. Adjusted amount = amount × 337.511 ÷ the CPI-U of its own year, rounded to the nearest $100. The 2026 insured figure is a replacement-cost value from the current homeowners policy, not a market price; it is shown beside the sale prices for scale only, and it does not change with the switch. (The assessed 1922–1926 figures and the census-reported 1940 figure are converted by the same switch, with the CPI-U annual averages above. The disputed 1930 reading and the nominal-consideration rows are shown as written and are not converted: a $1 deed consideration is a legal formality, not a value, and the 1930 enumerator's overwritten digit has no single figure to convert.)

Chapter 1

Henry Call

The first owner is the book's first research frontier: a name, a former town, and a house — and, if one tantalizing lead holds, a business on the ice of Spy Pond.

What is actually confirmed about Henry Call is short. He was "formerly of Charlestown, Massachusetts" (per the National Register nomination), he was the house's original owner, and the house was "first occupied by Henry Call."Confirmed His dates, occupation, family, and death were not found in the sources available online.Not found

The lead: in their March 26, 2023 letter to the Arlington ZBA, the current owners wrote that "the original owner of our home was mentioned in a documentary making a business by harvesting ice from Spy Pond." The documentary is unidentified and the claim untested.Unproven If true, Call belongs in the Spy Pond ice trade — the industry that filled the pond below his new house with horse teams, ice houses, and a railroad siding every winter (see the Era Notes) — and possibly in the business records of the Frederic Tudor era.

The paper trail, 1852–1857 — from Russell's notes

Rob Russell's estate notes give the land a paper trail the online record never produced.Single secondary source — the notes; the deeds themselves not yet pulled In 1852, S. Timothy Swan sold parcels A, B, and C to Daniel Chamberlin, who sold them on the same year to Addison Gage — the Spy Pond ice dealer. The first available plan of the property, dated 1854, measures 39,992 square feet. In 1854 Gage sold parcel A — the house lot — to a man the notes name as Henry E. Cole. In 1855, documents re-register a mortgage to Addison Gage alone (it had run from "Gage, Layon, and Sawyer") by Henry Call — and, the notes stress, "for the first time buildings are mentioned — not just land." In 1857 Gage leased parcels B and C to Sarah Ann Burchard for 99 years at one cent a year: she could build nothing on the property, would pay the taxes, and would not interfere with ice harvesting.

Two things follow. First, the ice trade is in the deeds themselves: the 1857 lease's ice-harvesting clause, and a mortgage running from the ice partners Gage, Layon [Lyon?], and Sawyer, put the estate's shore parcels inside the working Spy Pond ice business in the very years the house went up — which firms up, without proving, the documentary lead below that Call himself was in that trade. Second, the first owner's name is now in open conflict: Cole (the 1854 sale, per the notes) versus Call (the 1855 mortgage, the National Register nomination, and all later research). Either two men were involved in 1854–55, or one name is a misreading of deed handwriting. Russell's own handwritten summary uses "Henry Call 1854–1880." The November 2026 verification pass tested the names against the records: the MHC Form B names the original owner Henry Call — Call, with no middle initial, and no Cole anywhere in the form — and no record read or indexed in that pass contains a Henry (E.) Cole connected to this house, while a real Henry E. Call is attested in the immediate area in user-contributed genealogy (Henry Edwin Call, who married his cousin Emily Payson Call of the Charlestown family of Jonathan Call about 1849; in Jonathan Call's Charlestown household in 1850 and in Cambridge in 1860 — locator context only; it does not prove he built 216 Pleasant). Assessment, as far as the evidence reaches: the "Cole" reading currently has no documentary support at all, and "Call" is supported by the MHC form, the house's historic name, and the attested Charlestown-area Henry E. Call. But the one-man-or-two question cannot be settled without the deed. The 1850 census test is now complete (see the Hill section below): the entire West Cambridge schedule on NARA reel M432-324 — families 1–402, every page read from the page images — contains no Henry Call, no Henry E. Cole, no Burchard, no Corey, and no Gage Confirmed — from the record itself. Henry Call was therefore not living in West Cambridge in 1850, four years before he bought the estate in 1854; the “formerly of Charlestown” report remains the live lead for where he came from. The settling records remain: the original 1854 Gage deed and the 1855 mortgage document at the Middlesex South Registry, read in person.

Arlington in Call's decade

When the house went up, the town was still West Cambridge: incorporated from Cambridge on February 27, 1807, it took the name Arlington only on April 30, 1867 (Belmont had split off in 1859). Population: 2,202 in 1850, 2,681 in 1860, 3,261 in 1870.Confirmed Spy Pond was already an industrial landscape — ice harvested from mid-century, the Spy Pond Water Company piping water to West Cambridge from 1850 (renamed the Arlington Lake Company in 1867) — and during the Civil War a training camp, Camp Sheppard, stood near the pond. How the war touched the Call household specifically is not found;Not found Arlington's Civil War enrollment lists in the town reports and the 1860/1870 census schedules for the household would say.

How the house passed to Bartlett — Corey and Hubbell

No deed, date, or price for a sale from Call (or his heirs) to George Bartlett was located online, and Russell's notes explain why: Bartlett did not buy from Call. The notes place an E. W. Corey at 216 in 1875 (218 was then a stable), and record that in 1886 John H. Hubbell sold "land with the buildings A, B, C" to George H. Bartlett.Hubbell sale: from Russell's notes alone So between Call/Cole (1854) and Bartlett (1886) sit at least Corey (in 1875) and Hubbell (owner, who sold in 1886). How and when Hubbell acquired the estate, the notes do not say. Russell's handwritten summary gives Bartlett "1880–1923," which suggests Bartlett may have occupied the house from about 1880 — as a tenant, perhaps — some years before he bought it; that would square with the nomination's "from the 1880s," and with the family still being in Somerville at the 1880 census if the move came after enumeration.Inference The settling records: the Middlesex South Registry of Deeds grantor and grantee indexes under Call, Corey, Hubbell, and Bartlett, c. 1854–1890, searched in person at 208 Cambridge Street, Cambridge (deed images before January 1974 are not online), corroborated by the Arlington directories of 1883 and 1890.

The Corey placement is now plate-confirmed — Beers Atlas, 1875

Corey's presence no longer rests on Russell's notes alone. F. W. Beers, County Atlas of Middlesex, Massachusetts (1875), Arlington village plate, printed pp. 103–104 (with the town plate p. 101), read from the Archive.org page images and archived in the project archive (maps-plans), letters “E. W. Corey” on a pond-side Pleasant Street parcel in the 216 stretch.Confirmed — the plate itself The Corey lot as drawn ran from Pleasant Street to the Spy Pond shore and carried two buildings — one at the street, one mid-lot on a dashed drive. That confirms, from a primary source, that E. W. Corey held a pond-side Pleasant Street parcel in this stretch in 1875.

What the plate does not by itself prove is the exact modern address. That the Corey lot is exactly today's 216 Pleasant Street is Inference — house numbering and the 1954–56 Hunter subdivision intervened, and only the deeds settle the lot equivalence. The inference is supported, not proved, by the plate's mid-lot building position, which is consistent with this house's set-back, elevated siting. Whether Corey owned or rented in the deed sense also remains for the registry to settle; the plate letters the holding in his name.

Observation, not a conclusion: the lot immediately south of Corey's was lettered “Mrs. M. Payson,” with First Cong. Society / N. Pratt Est. in the same southern group — a Payson holding beside the Corey/Call parcel. The Call family's own history, as noted above, includes an Emily Payson Call connection. No kinship between Mrs. M. Payson and that family is shown on the plate, and none is asserted here.

The 1870 Census — “E. W. Corey” is Elijah Willis Corey

The 1870 U.S. Census for Arlington (NARA M593 roll 622, written page 34, enumerated July 29, 1870) now gives Corey his full name and his household.Confirmed The atlas's “E. W. Corey” is Elijah Willis Corey, 28, a leather dealer born in Illinois, living with his wife Oceanna (28, born Massachusetts), son Willis C. (3), daughter Emma H. (2), and two Irish domestic servants, Bridget Dowd and Bridget Horn. The next household enumerated was Charles O. Gage, ice dealer — the same Gage–Corey adjacency the 1875 atlas shows.Confirmed

Corey's wife is now identified by her maiden name.Confirmed — index grade In the Massachusetts Archives' official vital-records index, the bride-side marriage entry “Cooke, Oceanna M., Cambridge, 1864, Vol. 172, p. 52” carries the exact register citation of the groom-side entry “Corey, E. Willis, Cambridge, 1864, Vol. 172, p. 52” — so Elijah Willis Corey married Oceanna M. Cooke at Cambridge in 1864. The shared citation is what pairs the two entries; the register page itself (Vol. 172, p. 52) is the settling read and has not yet been read. The identification also supports a death candidate for her, carried as a candidate only: “Oceanna M. (Cooke) Corey,” Boston, 1906, Vol. 13, p. 364.Unproven — index-grade candidate

The same census settles the timing of the handover before Corey. Charles Birchard — the wholesale grocer listed at the house in the 1869–70 directory — appears nowhere in the entire 1870 Arlington census.Confirmed The Birchard-to-Corey handover at the house therefore falls in 1869–1870.

One limit must be stated plainly: the 1870 census records no street addresses, so the census itself does not name this house. That Corey's enumerated household is the 216 Pleasant household is Inference — not census fact — resting on the atlas lettering, the directories, and the Gage adjacency described above.

The Cambridge Directory for 1872 — Corey gone from Cambridge

One further directory check brackets Corey from the Cambridge side. The Cambridge Directory for 1872 (printed p. 100; page image archived in the project archive) no longer lists Elijah Willis Corey in Cambridge: the book's only Corey is an unrelated Amelia Corey.Confirmed That absence is consistent with his move to Arlington by 1870 — the 1870 census (above) already places him there. See ledger Item 31.

The 1880 Census — Corey gone from Arlington

The 1880 U.S. Census for Arlington has now been read in full from the NARA page images (T9 roll 540, enumeration districts 386 and 387).Confirmed No Corey household appears anywhere in either district — Elijah Willis Corey was no longer living in Arlington by June 1880. His Arlington residency therefore now brackets to 1870 through sometime before June 1880. This does not rule out his still owning the Pleasant Street house as an absentee; ownership can only be settled by the deed.

His 1870 next-door neighbour was still there. Charles O. Gage was still on Pleasant Street in 1880 (ED 387, p. 37, dwelling 290): age 44, a merchant, with wife Charlotte L., son Robert (17), and daughters Charlotte L. (10) and Ruth A. (6).Confirmed

In the 1880 visitation order, the household enumerated immediately before Gage's was Jonathan Pettengill's — the same position Corey occupied in 1870 — so Pettengill is a possible occupant (perhaps a tenant) of the Call house in 1880.Inference This is a positional match only and is not proven.

Who sold the house to George Bartlett therefore remains Unproven at the deed level. Homer's 1912 manuscript chain — Call → Burchard → Corey → Bartlett — stays labelled as manuscript-level, not deed-verified (see the manuscript section below).

The 1880 Census — Corey found in Charlestown

The 1880 U.S. Census for Boston's Charlestown district (ED 616, page 21, enumerated June 7, 1880) has now located Corey himself.Confirmed He is enumerated at City Square — Waverley Block, Charlestown, a leather dealer born in Illinois, living with his wife — entered as “Willie C,” age 30, born Massachusetts — and two sons: Chester, 7, and a 13-year-old son whose initials read H. C. (possibly W. C.). The placement matches his 1880 Boston directory entry giving his home as the Waverley House, Charlestown (see “After Arlington,” below).Confirmed

Three discrepancies against the 1870 census are flagged here, not harmonized:Unproven / open Corey's age reads 33, against 28 in the 1870 census; his wife is not entered under the name Oceanna, his wife in the 1870 census; and his daughter Emma H., aged 2 in 1870, does not appear in the 1880 household. No explanation for any of the three is offered here.

After Arlington — Boston and Dorchester, 1880–1896

Where Corey went next is now documented year by year. The Boston city directories for 1880–1886 and the Dorchester Blue Book for 1885 — all read from the page images and archived in the project archive — trace him after Arlington.Confirmed In 1880 he was a partner in Corey & Bond, horse equipments, at 234/236 Purchase Street, Boston, and was living at the Waverley House in Charlestown. In 1881–1883 he was dealing in hides and leather — at 140 Pearl, then 224 Congress, then 34 High — and living at the Hotel Falmouth. In 1884 his trade had changed to games and novelties at 133 Pearl; he was still at the Hotel Falmouth. In 1885 his business was still at 133 Pearl, but his house was now 8 Batchelder Street, Dorchester — the 1885 Dorchester Blue Book lists him there under his full name, “Elijah Willis Corey.” In 1886 he is listed at 8 Batchelder with no business address printed. See ledger Item 32.

The trace now extends one year further. The Boston Directory for 1887 (printed p. 289) lists:Confirmed

“Corey E. Willis (Corey & Andrews), 86 Bedford, h. 8 Batchelder”

— Boston Directory, 1887, printed p. 289

The firm Corey & Andrews sold boot and shoe machinery at 86 Bedford Street, Boston, and Corey still lived at 8 Batchelder Street, Dorchester.Confirmed The same page gives his son's first record since childhood:

“Corey Willis C. messenger, Blackstone Nat. Bank, bds. 8 Batchelder”

— Boston Directory, 1887, printed p. 289

Willis C. Corey (born about 1867 — the young child, age 3, in the 1870 Arlington census household above) was a messenger at the Blackstone National Bank boarding at his father's house at 8 Batchelder.Confirmed This is Willis C.'s first appearance in a record since 1870. See ledger Item 33.

And the run does not end there — 1887–88 is not Corey's endpoint. He is absent from the 1888 Boston directory, but that absence was a one-year omission, not his death or departure: the Boston Directory for 1889 lists him again, and the directory for 1890 lists him once more at the same address and in the same role (page images archived in the project archive):Confirmed

“Corey E. Willis, supt. h. 8 Batchelder, Dor.”

— Boston Directory, 1889

The 1890 directory carries him at 8 Batchelder Street, Dorchester in the same role, “supt.”Confirmed His son is with him in both years: Willis C. Corey, messenger at the Blackstone National Bank, boards at 8 Batchelder in 1889 and again in 1890.Confirmed A third Corey boards at the house in both years as well — Chester Corey, clerk. No record read states Chester's relationship to Elijah Willis or to Willis C., so he is entered here as a household member only: Inference / Unproven — not a proven son. Corey's Boston-directory run therefore now spans 1880–1890, with only the 1888 gap. His death, and any later endpoint after 1890, were then unplaced — the Suffolk probate index has since closed the death to “by 1891” (see the probate entry immediately below); the exact death date remains Not found. See ledger Item 35.

The Suffolk probate index — a will probated in 1891

The official Index to the Probate Records of the County of Suffolk, Massachusetts, 1636–1893, Vol. 1 (A–F), printed p. 239, lists:Confirmed

“1891 — Corey, E. Willis — will — No. 86371”

— Index to the Probate Records of Suffolk County, Vol. 1, printed p. 239

Elijah Willis Corey therefore left a will probated in Suffolk County in 1891 (case No. 86371), which confirms he had died by 1891.Confirmed That is consistent with the Boston directories: Corey himself is listed in 1890, and “Mrs. E. Willis Corey” heads the household in the listings that follow (below). The exact death date and the contents of the will file remain Unproven / not yet read — the index entry is what has been read, not the case file itself; Suffolk Probate case No. 86371 is the record that would give both.

The widow at 21 Sargent Street — the 1896 directory

The family's Dorchester trace continues past Elijah Willis Corey's own listings — as his widow's household. In the Boston Directory for 1896, the household was still at 21 Sargent Street, Dorchester: Mrs. E. Willis Corey is listed as the householder there, with Chester Corey, salesman, and Willis C. Corey, clerk at the Blackstone National Bank, boarding there.Confirmed Her tenure at that address now runs 1892–1896 in directory evidence — the 1896 listing extends it to that year. Willis C.'s bank is the same Blackstone National Bank at which he was a messenger in 1887 and in 1889–1890, now as a clerk; Chester, the clerk boarding at 8 Batchelder in 1889–1890, is now listed as a salesman — his relationship to the family remains unstated in any record read, so he stays a household member only: Inference / Unproven, not a proven son. Elijah Willis Corey's own death record — date and place — remains Not found: the widow listing confirms he had died by 1896, and the Suffolk probate index (above) narrows that to died by 1891, but neither gives the exact date or place. See ledger Item 38.

The 1900 Census — the widow named: Oceana Corey

The 1900 U.S. Census (Boston ED 1399, Sheet 16B, lines 81–82; NARA T623 roll 684; page image archived in the project archive) now identifies Corey's widow by name in a primary record for the first time.Confirmed She is Oceana Corey, born August 1841 in Massachusetts, enumerated in June 1900 as a widow living at 21 Sargent Street, Dorchester — the same address as the 1896 directory household above — in a home she owned free of mortgage, with her son Willis C. Corey (born June 1867), now a bank book keeper.Confirmed She is the same Oceana who appears as Elijah's wife in the 1870 Arlington census (above).

What remains unproven is stated plainly.Unproven / open Her maiden name is still unknown — no record read gives it. And the wife recorded with Elijah in the 1880 Charlestown census, read as “Willie/Nellie C,” age 30, does not match Oceana's age (she would have been 38 in 1880), so a possible second marriage in the 1870s remains an open question — flagged here, not resolved.

One thing the directories do not settle: where he and his family were enumerated in the 1880 census remains Unproven — a Charlestown hotel household, consistent with the Waverley House listing, is the lead, but no enumeration of the family has been identified.

The record that anchors this chapter

Mrs. Horace H. Homer's 1912 manuscript history of Pleasant Street, Pleasant Street — Ancient and Modern (Arlington Historical Society), discusses this house on page 26 — it is the nomination's own source for the Call era. Reading that page in full is the single most promising next step for Henry Call's story. A partial typed copy is at Digital Commonwealth (id 2012.6.112).

The manuscript has now been read — the chain before Bartlett

That reading has since been done. Mrs. Horace H. Homer, Pleasant Street — Ancient and Modern (1912), Arlington Historical Society manuscript — typewritten copy 1985.33.15 — treats this house under the heading “BARTLETT.” on printed p. 32, and states the ownership chain before Bartlett in so many words:Unproven — as stated by a contemporary 1912 local-history manuscript; not deed-proven Henry Call purchased the estate in 1854 from Mr. Hill, built the house, lived there a few years, then sold to Mr. Charles Burchard, who sold to Mr. Corey, from whom Prof. George Bartlett purchased it. On this account, Bartlett bought from Corey — not directly from Call — which fits the Corey placement the 1875 Beers plate confirms (above), though the manuscript gives no dates for the Burchard, Corey, or Bartlett transfers, and no deed for any link in this chain has yet been read.

The manuscript does not agree with this history's other leads, and the disagreements are recorded, not smoothed over. (1) Who sold to Call in 1854? Russell's notes (above) say Addison Gage sold the house lot to the 1854 buyer; the manuscript says Call purchased from Mr. Hill. Hill versus Gage is Unproven either way until the 1854 deed itself is read. (2) Who sold to Bartlett? Russell's notes record an 1886 sale by John H. Hubbell to Bartlett; the manuscript's chain — Call → Burchard → Corey → Bartlett — has no Hubbell in it. The Hubbell lead is contradicted by the manuscript but remains Unproven on the deed evidence, which has not been pulled for either account. (3) A citation mismatch in the record itself: the National Register form's bibliography cites this manuscript (as History of Pleasant Street Up Until 1912) at “p. 26,” but in the typewritten copy the Bartlett passage stands on printed p. 32, and p. 26 covers Peabody/Hicks. The mismatch is flagged here without resolving it — the nomination may have used a differently paginated copy, or the citation may simply be wrong; the manuscript itself is the same either way. See ledger Item 19.

Who was “Mr. Hill”? — the 1850 Census gives three candidates, and no answer yet

The search for Call's grantor has now reached the census schedules themselves — and the read is complete. The entire West Cambridge schedule in the 1850 U.S. Census on NARA microfilm reel M432-324 — families 1–402, every page read from the page images — has been read in full.Confirmed — from the record itself Written page 332 (image n320, archived in the project archive) shows a Hill cluster in consecutive households:Confirmed census facts

  • Amos Hill, 76 — with $8,000 in real estate.
  • Amos Hill Jr., 40, farmer — with $12,500 in real estate.
  • Henry W. Hill, 38, farmer — with $12,800 in real estate.

Any of the three could in principle be the “Mr. Hill” of the Homer manuscript — a substantial West Cambridge landholder selling an estate parcel in 1854 — but that identification is Unproven for each of them: no record yet says which Hill sold, and the manuscript gives no first name. The census facts themselves are confirmed; the candidacy is not. The 1854 deed, when read, is the record that would name the grantor.

The same page-by-page read has now tested the other names in the chain across the whole town — and the negative is complete, not partial. The entire 1850 schedule for West Cambridge — families 1–402, every page read from the page images — contains no Henry Call, no Henry E. Cole, no Burchard, no Corey, and no Gage.Confirmed — from the record itself Henry Call was therefore not living in West Cambridge in 1850, four years before he bought the estate in 1854; the earlier report that he was “formerly of Charlestown” remains the live lead for where he came from. Charles Burchard (who, per the Homer manuscript, bought the house from Call) and Sarah Ann Burchard likewise do not appear in West Cambridge in 1850, and neither does E. W. Corey, who held the lot by 1875. The Hills, by contrast, are there in force — Amos Hill, Amos Hill Jr., and Henry W. Hill among them (above) — the candidate pool for the “Mr. Hill” of the manuscript; which Hill sold is still Unproven. See ledger Items 12 and 26.

The Boston directories, 1861–1870 — Birchard and the Gages at West Cambridge

The Boston Directory evidence for both families now runs continuously through the decade. The Boston Directory run for Charles Birchard and for the Gage ice family is continuous 1861–1870 (page images read and archived in the project archive).Confirmed The run places both households at West Cambridge — the town that became Arlington in 1867 — years before the 1869–70 Arlington directory below names them on Pleasant Street.

For Birchard, the opening year is explicit. In the 1861 directory (printed p. 49):Confirmed

“Birchard Charles (B. & Torrey), house at West Cambridge”

— Boston Directory, 1861, printed p. 49

“Birchard & Torrey (C. Birchard and J. M. Torrey), grocers, 183 State”

— Boston Directory, 1861, printed p. 49

Birchard was therefore a Boston grocer — partner with J. M. Torrey in Birchard & Torrey, grocers, at 183 State Street — whose house was at West Cambridge in 1861, the same Boston business address, 183 State, that the 1869–70 directory still gives him (below).Confirmed

For the Gages, the 1862 directory (printed p. 161) gives both the firm and the man:Confirmed

“Gage Addison & Co. (C. O. Gage), ice, 70 State, house at West Cambridge”

— Boston Directory, 1862, printed p. 161

“Gage Charles O. (A. Gage & Co.), ice, 70 State, h. at W. Cambridge”

— Boston Directory, 1862, printed p. 161

One nuance must be stated plainly, because the two years do not say the same thing about Charles O. Gage personally. In 1861 his personal entry reads “h. at Charlestown” even though the firm's house is given as West Cambridge — he was still personally a Charlestown householder in 1861 and appears at West Cambridge from 1862.Confirmed The firm's West Cambridge house in 1861 is therefore not, by itself, proof of his personal residence there that year.

What the Boston run does not settle is the address. The directories give no West Cambridge street or house number for Birchard. Whether Charles Birchard's West Cambridge house was this house — today's 216 Pleasant — remains Inference, not Confirmed, resting as before on the Homer chain (Call → Birchard → Corey → Bartlett) read together with the later Arlington directory and the 1875 Beers plate; only the deeds settle which house he occupied. See ledger Item 49.

The 1869–70 directory — Charles Birchard on Pleasant Street

A second primary source now places the middle link of the Homer chain on Pleasant Street in person. The Somerville, Arlington and Belmont Directory for 1869–70 (Dudley & Greenough, 1869; Archive.org item arlingtoncitydir1869arli), read from its own page images (archived in the project archive), lists on p. 162:Confirmed — from the directory itself

“Birchard Charles, wholesale grocer (183 State, B.), house Pleasant, near Spy Pond”

— Directory, p. 162

The spelling matters: the directory gives BIRCHARD, not the “Burchard” of the 1912 Homer manuscript (above). Whether the manuscript misspelled the name, or the directory did, the man is the same link in the chain — Charles, the buyer from Call in the manuscript's account, now found in a contemporary directory as a Boston wholesale grocer living on Pleasant Street near Spy Pond in 1869. A second entry fills out the household: p. 168 lists “Donnelly Patrick, gardener, Charles Birchard's, Pleasant”Confirmed — Birchard kept an estate on Pleasant Street with a resident gardener, Patrick Donnelly, in 1869, which fits a substantial house-and-grounds holding rather than a cottage.

That Birchard's Pleasant Street house was the Call house — today's 216 — is Inference, and it is labelled as such throughout this history: the directory gives no house numbers, only “Pleasant, near Spy Pond,” so the equivalence is not proven by the directory itself. The inference rests on the Homer chain (Call → Birchard → Corey → Bartlett) read together with the 1875 Beers plate, which puts Corey on the pond-side lot six years later; only the deeds settle which house Birchard occupied.

The directory's negative evidence is just as pointed, and it was verified, not assumed. Its Arlington C-section (pp. 164–166) was read in full: it contains no Corey or Cory entry and no Call entry.Not found — verified negative Neither E. W. Corey nor Henry Call was an Arlington resident in 1869. That is exactly what the Homer chain predicts — Call had already sold and left, and Corey had not yet arrived — and it brackets Corey's tenure from below: he appears as the lot's holder only by the 1875 Beers atlas (above), not in 1869.

The same pages confirm the street around him (see also Chapter 6). P. 170 lists “Gage Anna, widow Addison, house Pleasant, n. Spy Pond” — so Addison Gage, the ice dealer who assembled the estate parcels in 1852, was dead by 1869Confirmed — and “Gage Charles O. ice dealer (128 State, B.), house Pleasant, near Spy Pond.” The Middlesex probate index now fixes both Gages' endpoints (see Chapter 6): Anna's will was probated in 1886 (case No. 20272), so she died by 1886, and Charles O.'s in 1892 (case No. 31715), so he died by 1892.Confirmed — index-grade P. 176 lists “Libby Jackson H. foreman of ice business for Addison, Gage & Co.” — the Gage ice business was still operating under Addison's name after his death. And pp. 172–173 list Charles Hill, George Hill, and Mary Hill, all living on Pleasant near the pond — the Hill family still on the street fifteen years after one of them, on the manuscript's account, sold the estate to Call.

One name the directory does not settle is the lessee of 1857. Sarah Ann Burchard, who took the 99-year lease of parcels B and C from Gage in Russell's notes, may be recorded under the spelling “Birchard” — the spelling the directory uses for Charles. Searches under both spellings have so far found no matching person, and her identity — including any kinship to Charles Birchard — remains Unproven / open. See ledger Item 27.

Chapter 2

The Bartlett era, 1880s–1924

For more than forty years this was the home of George Hartnell Bartlett — English lithographer, maker of pictorial maps of three capitals, and for twenty-nine years the principal of the Massachusetts State Normal Art School. His is the tenure the house is named for, and the centerpiece of its history.

The man

George Hartnell Bartlett was born May 24, 1838, in Camberwell, London, and died at this house in 1923 — on March 26, per Geographicus (and his Boston Globe obituary). The MHC Form B / National Register nomination gives March 29, citing the Arlington Advocate of March 30, 1923, p. 4, col. 2. The November 2026 verification pass reports both dates and does not pick one: the conflict is documented, not settled. The settling record — the Massachusetts death register for 1923, Arlington (Massachusetts Archives, which holds deaths 1841–1935; imaged in FamilySearch's "Massachusetts Deaths, 1841-1915, 1921-1924," collection 1463156) — was not read, and his Mount Pleasant Cemetery burial record remains a companion check.Confirmed, one date in dispute One secondary source places him "from Brayton, Surrey" — inconsistent with the Camberwell birth given by Geographicus and by Men of Massachusetts ("Born, London, Eng., May 24, 1838"); treat it as garbled.Unproven

He studied engineering, mastered printing and lithography, and is credited with pioneering the steam press in London around 1867. His name is sometimes misprinted "C. H. Bartlett" — a standing warning for anyone searching indexes for him. He was naturalized a U.S. citizen on October 24, 1887, having applied in 1883.Confirmed The verification pass identified the correct index for that naturalization — the Index to New England Naturalization Records, 1791–1906 (NARA microfilm M1299, RG 85; FamilySearch collection 1840474), whose cards give name, residence, court, and certificate volume/page — but Bartlett's card itself was not retrieved. Expectation, per the pass: pre-1906 petitions normally do not record arrival date or ship; those fields are a feature of post-1906 petitions, so the card, when pulled, will likely show court and certificate data only. One same-name man is explicitly rejected: a Fold3 petition for a George Bartlett of Newfoundland, immigrated 1895, petition dated February 3, 1914 — not the English-born, 1870-arrival Arlington Bartlett.

A career in three cities

London, 1867. His first and most significant work: a pictorial "monumental-style" Illustrated Map of London, published by Smith & Son — a bird's-eye street map studded with little drawings of the city's public buildings. The only cataloged example a dealer could cite sits at the Aargauer Kantonsbibliothek in Aarau, Switzerland (OCLC 1245126693). In London he also produced tinted lithographs after John Gibbs for Gibbs' Studies for Art Designers and Manufacturers (cataloged at the Yale Center for British Art, with Ensor & Simkins).

New York, 1870. He emigrated in May 1870 and set up at 309 Broadway, partnering with Major and Knapp on a pictorial map of New York.

Boston, 1871. Family tradition, via Geographicus, says he answered a newspaper advertisement for a teaching job while visiting Boston — and stayed. He made a pictorial map of Boston in 1871 and an Illustrated Map of Paris in 1877. In 1872 he was principal of the South Boston School of Art.

The Normal Art School

In 1873 Bartlett was invited — without competition, by John Philbrick, chairman of the Board of Visitors — to be the first instructor of the new Massachusetts State Normal Art School (today the Massachusetts College of Art and Design, founded 1873, still the only publicly funded independent art school in the United States). The school existed because the Massachusetts Drawing Act of May 16, 1870 — the first such state mandate in the country — had made drawing instruction obligatory in the public schools, and someone had to train the teachers. Bartlett also became principal of Boston's evening drawing schools, a post he held 36 years, until 1908. After ten years of teaching he became the school's principal, 1883–1912, and thereafter Principal Emeritus, lecturing on lithography and the modern reproductive processes. He was a leading member of the Boston Lithographic Artists' Association.Confirmed

A trap in the sources — "first principal"?

A Massachusetts Board of Library Commissioners guide calls Bartlett "the first principal of the Massachusetts Normal Art School (now MassArt)" and a teacher of Edmund C. Tarbell. The school's own 1917 yearbook biography instead makes him first instructor (1873) and principal only after a decade, and MassArt names its first dormitory Walter Smith Hall, for its founding principal Walter Smith. The defensible formulation: Smith founded and first led the school; Bartlett was its first instructor and its principal from 1883 to 1912. The MassArt Archives catalogs and Board of Education annual reports, 1873–1912, would settle it outright.

After a decade in rented rooms — Pemberton Square, School Street, the Deacon House on Washington Street — the school got its first purpose-built home in 1886 at Newbury and Exeter Streets, Boston: the building of Bartlett's principalship. The surviving catalogs (1892–93 through 1904) list him teaching Modelling from the Antique Figure and Life, Historic Ornament and Design, Principles of Design in Nature, Drawing for Illustration, Process Engraving, and Blackboard Illustration. The school moved to the Longwood/Huntington campus in 1983.

The circle around the school

The Bartlett decades put 216 Pleasant on a commuting line into Boston's art world. People in the school's orbit, each confirmed individually and each a thread a fuller history can pull:

  • Walter Smith — the school's founding principal, Bartlett's predecessor.
  • John Philbrick — chairman of the Board of Visitors, who recruited Bartlett in 1873.
  • Cyrus Dallin — the sculptor taught at the school; the Cyrus Dallin Art Museum in Arlington documents his long commute.
  • George Loftus Noyes — the painter studied with Bartlett before leaving for Paris in 1890.
  • Sears Gallagher — the etcher trained under Bartlett at the Hawes Evening Drawing School, Boston, 1882–86.
  • John H. Garo — the photographer won the Photographers' Association of New England gold medal in 1914 for his portrait of Bartlett — the best portrait lead for this house's most documented resident.
  • Sigfrid N. Mellin — maker of the 52 plates in Bartlett's Pen and Ink Drawing.
  • Charles E. Adams — the woodcarver studied drawing under Bartlett (Winterthur, Joseph Downs Collection finding aid).

One further credit — that Bartlett modeled the posthumous plaster bust of Chaplain Fuller presented to the State House — comes from a State Library document whose snippet dates the presentation to 1863, before his 1870 immigration. It is garbled as it stands and should not be used until the original document is read.Unproven

His works — a checklist

  • Illustrated Map of London (1867), pub. Smith — pictured above. Geographicus
  • Pictorial map of New York (1870, with Major and Knapp) — repository copy to be located; the NYPL Map Division is the obvious check.
  • Pictorial map of Boston (1871) — repository copy to be located; Leventhal Map Center.
  • Illustrated Map of Paris, or Stranger's Guide… (Boston, 1877) — page images at HathiTrust.
  • The Public Schools of Massachusetts (Boston, 1893) — "designed and drawn by George H. Bartlett"; copies at the BPL Leventhal Center (G3761.E68 1893 .B37), Brown, the State Library of Massachusetts, and the Newberry; OCLC 60426210. Geographicus
  • The Public Libraries of Massachusetts (1893; another edition Arlington, Mass.: G. H. Bartlett, c.1904) — the 1904 edition was published from Arlington: documentary proof of Bartlett working from this house's town in his retirement years. Digital Commonwealth
  • Pen and Ink Drawing (Cambridge: Riverside Press, 1903), viii + 223 pp., 52 plates by Sigfrid N. Mellin — praised in the school's student paper The Center of Vision (Feb. 1904) as "the best manual yet published." HathiTrust catalog 001989518.
  • A portrait with likeness in Men of Massachusetts, Part 6 — text online.

Julia Louisa and the thirteen children

George's wife was Julia Louisa Bartlett. The one consolidated source for the family is the askART biography credited to genealogist Sandi Hartnell — a family researcher's secondary account, valuable and untested. It gives Julia's maiden name as Julia Louisa Smith. That name was long carried here as unproven; a later FreeBMD search has now found a strong index-grade candidate that supports it — see below — but the marriage is not Confirmed until the certificate itself is read.

The marriage — a strong 1857 candidate: George Hartnell Bartlett and Julia Louisa Smith

A live FreeBMD search of GRO marriages (Bartlett, George, spouse first name Julia, 1855–1863) returned exactly two matches, and its first match is the strongest marriage candidate yet found:Unproven — strong index-grade candidate, not Confirmed

  • December quarter 1857, Newington, vol. 1d, page 347 — the index entry reads “Bartlett, George Hartnell.” The four entries on that index page are George Hartnell Bartlett, Ann Harvey, Elias Morton, and Julia Louisa Smith — the page's only Julia.

Why this candidate is strong: George's full Hartnell name appears in the groom entry; the bride's names, Julia Louisa, match his wife Julia Louisa (Julia L.); the Dec 1857 date fits the marriage of about 1858 that both the 1900 census (married 42 years) and the 1910 census (married 52 years) report; and Newington lies in South London adjoining Camberwell, George's birthplace. Together these make the Newington entry a very strong candidate for the couple's marriage, and for Julia's maiden name being Smith. Why it is still not proof: a GRO index page does not state which groom married which bride — the other couple on the page is Elias Morton / Ann Harvey — so the index alone does not prove the pairing. Settling record: the GRO marriage certificate for Dec 1857, Newington, vol. 1d, p. 347 — not yet obtained; Julia's Massachusetts death certificate (below) would corroborate via her parents' names.

The two candidates the November 2026 completion pass had isolated are now displaced by the 1857 entry, which predates them and carries George's full Hartnell name. FreeBMD, searched live in that pass (freebmd.org.uk), had returned exactly two marriages of a George Bartlett to a bride named Julia in 1860–1870:Confirmed as to what the index returns

  • June quarter 1862, Bermondsey, vol. 1d, page 103 — page-mates: Bartlett, George; Chamberlain, Mary Ann; Green, Edwin Theophilas [Theophilus] Smith; and Sherriff, Julia.
  • December quarter 1866, Barnet, vol. 3a, page 185 — page-mates: BARTLETT, George; Clark, Julia; Knight, James C.; SKELTON, Mary.

Each GRO page holds two couples, so the index alone cannot pair George with Julia Sherriff (1862) versus Julia Clark (1866) versus the non-Julia brides on the same pages — and both entries in any case post-date the censuses' marriage date of about 1858, while their groom entries give “George” alone, without the Hartnell name the 1857 entry carries. A separate FreeBMD search for George Bartlett marriages, March 1863–December 1866, returned 42 entries, none entered as “George Hartnell Bartlett” — the GRO index gives “George” alone (plus Scott/White/James/Walter/Thomas/Henry/W/L/R variants). London-area entries in that search included Richmond S. Jun 1863 2a 408; Marylebone Mar 1864 1a 767 and Mar 1865 1a 819; Poplar Mar 1866 1c 974; Clerkenwell Jun 1866 1b 944; and Barnet Dec 1866 3a 185.

Analysis: the conflict flagged when the 1900 census was read — its “married 42 years” (c. 1857–58) and Edward's July 1861 birth sitting uneasily with the 1862 and 1866 entries — is resolved in favour of the census by the 1857 candidate: a Dec 1857 marriage matches the censuses' figure and precedes Edward's 1861 birth. The earlier circumstantial points for Bermondsey 1862 (it adjoins Camberwell; it precedes Julia Lavinia, b. 1866) are superseded by the same points holding more strongly for Newington 1857. A FreeBMD births search (Bartlett, mother's surname Clark, 1862–1870) returned no matches, and FreeBMD itself notes the pre-1911 GRO birth index does not give mother's maiden name, so that route cannot discriminate. Settling record still needed: the GRO marriage certificate for Dec 1857, Newington, vol. 1d, p. 347 (or the parish register entry), or Julia's Massachusetts death certificate (below). Until one is read, the marriage and the maiden name Smith stand as a strong index-grade candidate, not Confirmed.Unproven — strong index-grade candidate See “The 1900 Census” subsection below and ledger Item 30.

GRO birth-index entries — George, Julia, and Edward (FreeBMD, index grade)

Three GRO birth-index entries, found via FreeBMD, are now recorded at index grade. They are index entries only — not certificates: the index gives name, registration district, quarter, volume, and page, and none of the birth certificates themselves has been read.Confirmed — as index entries

  • Julia Louisa Smith — GRO Births Sep 1839, St Saviour's, vol. 4, p. 423. This is the only Julia Louisa Smith birth entry in 1838–1840, and it fits Julia Bartlett's census birth of July 1839 (1900 census, above). At index grade it supports that George Hartnell Bartlett's wife was Julia Louisa Smith — the Julia Louisa Smith on the marriage index page for Dec 1857, Newington, vol. 1d, p. 347, where she is the only Julia on the page (see “The marriage” above). The marriage certificate itself has not been read and the index does not state pairings, so the pairing remains index-grade, not proven.Unproven — strong index-grade candidate, not Confirmed
  • George Hartnell Bartlett — GRO Births Sep 1838, Camberwell, vol. 4, p. 143 — the birth-index entry under his full Hartnell name, in the Camberwell district given elsewhere as his birthplace.Confirmed — as index entry
  • Edward Henry Hartnell Bartlett — GRO Births Sep 1861, Camberwell, vol. 1d, p. 455. The entry gives Edward H. H. Bartlett's full name as Edward Henry Hartnell Bartlett, matching his July 1861 census birth (1900 census, above).Confirmed — as index entry
