Secondary corroboration of the death date only: Geographicus gives “George Hartnell Bartlett (May 24, 1838 – March 26, 1923)… died at his home in Arlington, Massachusetts, in 1923” — a secondary source, not hard evidence.

The household and the estate in these years

The Arlington Historical Society holds a photograph cataloged "Bartlett Homestead, 216 Pleasant St," record 2007.1.52, dated 1920–1942 — the era's key image of the house. It was not located online in the earlier searches: a Digital Commonwealth search for "Bartlett Homestead" returned nothing, and the AHS PastPerfect catalog had to be searched directly by record number.Not found online — earlier searches; since read, below The Form B's bibliography, as printed on the form itself (reported in full by the verification pass), is: History of Pleasant Street Up Until 1912, p. 26; 1875 Beers & Co. Atlas; Menotomy Historical Districts Report, pp. 41–48; 1884 Bird's Eye View of Arlington; Arlington Advocate, p. 4, col. 2, March 30, 1923; Arlington Advocate 1898; Stadley & Co. Atlas; 1923 Sanborn Map Co. Atlas; Arlington Directories of 1869/70, 1883, 1890, 1898, 1923. Those anchor the rest of the visual record (the Sanborn Arlington editions run 1885–1973; the 1923 plate covering Pleasant Street should be verified on the plate itself). Which servants staffed the house, how the stables and gardens were kept, and how the family used Spy Pond are all recoverable from the census schedules named above — and all still unextracted.

The “Bartlett Homestead” photograph — record now read

The PastPerfect record has now been read directly.Confirmed Arlington Historical Society PastPerfect record 2007.1.52 is titled “Big Book p.52” (1920–1942, 8 images). Its image 8 is captioned “Bartlett Homestead, 216 Pleasant St” and shows the house from the street — white two-story clapboard, two chimneys, trees, a utility pole, and a 1940s car in front. This is the photograph the earlier searches could not surface; the record itself, read by its accession number, settles its title, date range, image count, and the caption and content of image 8. The image is CC BY-NC-ND, with rights status not evaluated — it is described here, not reproduced. See ledger Item 18 and Plates item 2.

The 1894 directory — the Bartletts at 88 Pleasant Street

The Arlington Directory for 1894 lists the household at this house in the middle of Bartlett's principalship. On printed p. 21 it gives “Prof. George H. Bartlett, principal of the Normal Art School (studio 27 Tremont, Boston), at house 88 Pleasant Street,” with Edward H. Bartlett at 88 Pleasant and Ethel G. Bartlett boarding there; the Pleasant Street list on printed p. 116 places the Bartletts at 88 Pleasant as well.Confirmed The numbering needs stating honestly: 88 was the house's number under the 1890s street numbering, and equating 88 Pleasant with today's 216 Pleasant rested, on the 1894 page alone, on the Bartletts' continuous occupancy of the house — a gap the 1900 directory has since closed (next subsection): the directories themselves now show the equivalence. The same directory carries a second, negative finding: no Corey appears anywhere in the 1894 directory,Confirmed extending E. Willis Corey's absence from the Arlington directories to 1883–1894 — since extended to 1883–1900 by the 1900 directory (next subsection). Source: The Arlington Directory for 1894, printed p. 21 and the Pleasant Street list on printed p. 116; the 1894 directory page images (printed pp. 21, 26–32, 116) are archived in the project archive.

The 1900 directory — the house becomes 216 Pleasant Street

The Arlington and Belmont Directory for 1900 (Edward A. Jones, copyright 1900; Archive.org item arlingtoncitydir1900arli; page images archived in the project archive), read from its own pages, gives the house its modern number for the first time in any record found.Confirmed Printed p. 22 lists “George H. Prof., principal Normal Art school (studio 27 Tremont, B.), h. 216 Pleasant,” and boarding at 216 Pleasant: Edward H. Bartlett; Ernest S. Bartlett, clerk; Ethel G. Bartlett, art teacher; and Julia L. Bartlett (Miss). The book's Pleasant Street list (printed p. 172) repeats 216 for Prof. & Mrs. George H. Bartlett, Edward H. Bartlett, and Miss Julia L. Bartlett — set between 208 (Freeman N. Young; Frank E. Thompson) and 226 (Samuel G. Prentiss).

The renumbering is now shown, not inferred. Pleasant Street was renumbered between the 1894 directory — where the Bartletts were at 88 Pleasant (above) — and 1900, and the same household appears at both numbers, with the same Prentiss neighbor beside it: Samuel G. Prentiss at 92 in 1894 and at 226 in 1900. The 88 = 216 equivalence is therefore shown by the directories themselves.Confirmed One identification in the entry is labelled honestly: that Julia L. Bartlett (Miss) is George's daughter Julia Lavinia Bartlett is Inference — the directory lists her at the house but does not state the relationship. The same directory carries the standing negative finding forward: its Arlington list's C section was read in full and contains no Corey or Cory — the book's only Corey entry is in its Belmont section, a different town — so E. Willis Corey's absence from the Arlington directories now extends to 1883–1900.Confirmed See ledger Item 29.

The 1900 Census — the household at 216 Pleasant, June 1, 1900

The census schedule for the house in the same year has now been read from the page image: 1900 U.S. Census, Arlington, ED 658, Sheet 1B (NARA T623 roll 655), enumerated June 1, 1900; the page image is archived in the project archive.Confirmed — from the census page itself At 216 Pleasant Street — dwelling 18, family 19 — the enumerator entered:

  • George H. Bartlett, head — born May 1835, England; immigrated 1866; naturalized; occupation Teacher of Art; the home owned, with a mortgage.
  • Julia L. Bartlett, wife — born July 1839, England; married 42 years; immigrated 1870; and the census's own figures for her: 13 children born, 9 living.
  • Edward H. H. Bartlett, son — born July 1861, England; immigrated 1872.
  • Julia L. Bartlett, daughter — born January 1866, England; artist in lithography.
  • Ethel G. Bartlett, daughter — born August 1867, England; Teacher of Art.
  • Ernest S. Bartlett, son — born October 1875, Massachusetts.
  • George S. F. Bartlett, son — born September 1880, Massachusetts; at school.
  • Annie E. Blake, boarder — born September 1845, Massachusetts; Teacher of Art.

Three things this page settles. First, Edward's relationship: he is entered explicitly as George's son — the relationship the May 1, 1909 poll list (above) left unstated is now resolved, and at July 1861 he is the eldest known Bartlett child.Confirmed Second, a new child: George S. F. Bartlett (b. September 1880, Massachusetts, at school) appears in no earlier list read for this history — he is a newly identified Bartlett child.Confirmed Third, Julia's own count: the census's figures for her — 13 children born, 9 living — are now on the record from the schedule itself, matching the thirteen of the family account.Confirmed

Annie E. Blake — the boarder identified as Bartlett's faculty colleague

The boarder on the schedule — Annie E. Blake, born September 1845, Massachusetts, Teacher of Art — is now identified from the school's own catalogue. The Massachusetts Normal Art School catalogue for 1899–1900, on its Instructors page, lists, under Principal George H. Bartlett:Confirmed

“ANNIE E. BLAKE — Modelling and Casting; Design in the Round.”

— Massachusetts Normal Art School catalogue, 1899–1900, Instructors page

Annie E. Blake was therefore Bartlett's faculty colleague at the Massachusetts Normal Art School in the year she boarded at 216 — a colleague living with the principal.Confirmed The identification rests on the catalogue citation above read with the census entry (same name, same occupation, same year, boarding in the principal's house). Her faculty tenure is now confirmed through 1915–16, and it ends there. The HathiTrust full-view Massachusetts Normal Art School catalogues (vols. 33–39, New York Public Library copy, item nyp.33433091420632) list “ANNIE E. BLAKE — Modeling and Casting; Design in the Round” on the Instructors page of every yearly catalogue from 1905/06 through 1911/12, and her verified catalogue tenure now runs in full from 1892–93 through 1915–16.Confirmed The end is fixed by the school's Class of 1917 Year Book: its officers list, read from the page images, contains no Annie E. Blake — Cyrus E. Dallin heads Modeling, and Raymond Porter teaches Modeling and Casting / Design in Relief, her former subjects.Confirmed The Mrs. Agnes Blake who does appear in that list is a different person, not merged with her here. Her birth and death records and her later life remain Not found — no record for them is stated here. See ledger Items 34 and 41.

The census also records the family's immigration years as staggered: George 1866, Julia 1870, Edward 1872, and the daughters (Julia L. and Ethel G.) 1874. They are reported here exactly as the census records them, without explanation.Confirmed as recorded

The census's “married 42 years” points to a marriage of c. 1857–58 — the date that sat uneasily with the two GRO candidates first isolated (Bermondsey, June 1862, Julia Sherriff; Barnet, December 1866, Julia Clark) but that now fits the strong index-grade candidate found since: Newington, Dec 1857 (George Hartnell Bartlett / Julia Louisa Smith, 1d 347) (see “The marriage” above). Edward's birth in July 1861 follows that marriage. Julia's maiden name Smith is therefore a strong candidate, not yet proven — the Newington certificate has not been obtained, and a GRO index page does not state which groom married which bride.Unproven — strong index-grade candidate, not Confirmed See ledger Item 30.

The 1910 Census — the household at 216 Pleasant, April 15, 1910

The next census schedule for the house has now been read: 1910 U.S. Census, Arlington, ED 728, Sheet 1A, enumerated April 15, 1910.Confirmed At 216 Pleasant Street the enumerator entered:

  • George H. Bartlett, head — 71; occupation Professor, Normal Art School.
  • Julia Bartlett, wife — 70; married 52 years; and again the census's own figures for her: 13 children born, 9 living — unchanged from 1900.
  • Edward H. Bartlett, son — 46.
  • Ethel G. Bartlett, daughter — 42; Teacher, Art School.
  • Annie E. Blake, boarder — 65; Teacher, Art School — Bartlett's faculty colleague (see the Blake subsection above), still boarding at 216 a decade on.

Three of the 1900 household are gone: Julia L., Ernest S., and George S. F. Bartlett do not appear in the 1910 household at 216.Confirmed The schedule does not say where they went, and no destination is stated here.

One conflict is flagged, not harmonized.Unproven / open The immigration years in the 1910 schedule conflict with the 1900 census: George is entered as immigrating in 1870 (1900: 1866), Julia in 1871 (1900: 1870), and Ethel in 1873 (1900: 1874). Both sets of figures are reported as recorded; neither is preferred here. What the two censuses do agree on is the marriage: “married 42 years” in 1900 and “married 52 years” in 1910 both point to a marriage of about 1858 — the c. 1857–58 date that fits the strong index-grade candidate found since, Newington, Dec 1857 (George Hartnell Bartlett / Julia Louisa Smith, 1d 347), and displaces the two later GRO entries (1862 and 1866; see “The marriage” above). The pairing itself remains unproven until the Newington certificate is read.Unproven — strong index-grade candidate, not Confirmed See ledger Item 40.

The 1920 Census — the household at 216 Pleasant, February 17, 1920

The last census schedule of the Bartlett era for the house has now been read: 1920 U.S. Census, Arlington, ED 4, Sheet 61A (NARA T625 roll 706), enumerated February 17, 1920.Confirmed At 216 Pleasant Street — dwelling 825, family 1486 — the enumerator entered:

  • George H. Bartlett, head — 81; born England; occupation teacher at the Normal Art School; the home owned.
  • Julia Bartlett, wife — 80; born England.
  • Ethel G. Bartlett, daughter — 50; single; born England; occupation teacher of art at the Normal Art School.

Five people from the earlier households at 216 are gone: Edward H. H. Bartlett, Julia L. Bartlett, Ernest S. Bartlett, George S. F. Bartlett, and boarder Annie E. Blake do not appear in the 1920 household at 216.Confirmed The schedule does not say where they went, and no destination is stated here.

Two conflicts are flagged, not harmonized.Inference / conflict The sheet writes a naturalization year of 1885 for all three Bartletts, which conflicts with the October 24, 1887 naturalization date given by other sources; and its immigration years — George 1870, Julia 1871, Ethel 1873 — conflict with the 1900 and 1910 censuses (1900: George 1866, Julia 1870, the daughters 1874; 1910: George 1870, Julia 1871, Ethel 1873). Both sets of figures are reported as recorded; neither is preferred here. See ledger Item 55.

After 1920 — the last Bartletts leave 216, and a banking namesake (unproven)

The Arlington True Lists close the Bartlett residence.Confirmed On April 1, 1924, Julia Bartlett, 84, was still at 216, with Ethel G. Bartlett, 56. By April 1, 1925, both are gone from 216 and the Hunter household is listed there. Julia's death or removal therefore falls in the window April 1924–April 1925; her Massachusetts death record itself remains Not found, and no death date is stated for her in this history. See ledger Item 56.

One forward trace for the youngest son is recorded — and deliberately not merged. A George S. F. Bartlett of Boston's Five Cent Savings Bank led a savings-bank conference in July 1922 (Oregon Daily Journal, July 16, 1922, p. 15).Unproven His identity with George S. F. Bartlett, son of George and Julia (b. September 1880; at 216 in 1900, absent in 1910 and 1920) is unproven — a shared, uncommon name-form is a lead, not proof — so the banker is not merged with the son here, and nothing about the son's life after 1900 is stated on the strength of the newspaper item. See ledger Item 57. The son himself is now identified in full from the primary-record indexes.Confirmed — index grade; page images not yet read He is George Stanley Fenwick Bartlett, born 10 September 1880 (WWI draft index; his draft registration was in Arlington, and the relative named is Alice R. Bartlett). The 1906 Cambridge marriage index entry (Vol. 563, p. 396) is his: he married Alice Rebecca Worcester on 25 October 1906 in Cambridge, and the index names his parents as George H. Bartlett and Julia L. Smith — independent corroboration, at index grade, that Julia's maiden name was Smith. What remains unproven is only the banker: whether this George Stanley Fenwick Bartlett is the Five Cents Savings Bank man of 1922 is still Unproven — the employer field on the unread draft-card image is the test that would settle it. A Find a Grave index lead (a lead, not evidence) gives his death as 17 February 1932, with burial at Winchester, Massachusetts.

George's Atlantic crossing — two candidates, both tested and rejected

The census above gives George's immigration year as 1866, and two Castle Garden-era passenger candidates for his crossing have now been tested against the records themselves — and both rejected. The index entry “George Bartlett, 26, arrived 1866, ship Tripoli” points to the manifest of the S.S. Tripoli, Liverpool & Queenstown to New York, list sworn July 30, 1866 (NARA microfilm M237, roll 268; the manifest page is archived in the project archive). Read on the page itself, that George Bartlett is a 26-year-old English laborer travelling in a party of five:Confirmed — from the manifest page itself

  • Edmund Bartlett, 63
  • Jane Bartlett, 62 — wife
  • George Bartlett, 26 — laborer
  • Elizabeth Bartlett, 25 — wife
  • Jane Bartlett, 1 — infant

Every particular conflicts with George H. Bartlett of this house: his wife was Julia Louisa, not Elizabeth; his eldest child, Edward, was born in England in 1861, not an infant Jane in 1866; he was an art teacher, not a laborer; and the 1900 census enters him as born in 1835, which would make him about 31 in 1866, not 26. The Tripoli record is therefore a tested-and-rejected same-name record — it documents a different George Bartlett's crossing, not this one's. See ledger Item 36.

The second candidate has now been read at manifest level as well — and it fails the same way. The passenger manifest of the City of London (NARA M237 roll 330; master Henry Tibbits; from London; sworn at New York June 1, 1870) lists at entry 54 a Geo. Bartlett, age 29, occupation farmer, travelling alone in steerage from Great Britain.Confirmed — from the manifest itself That man is not George H. Bartlett: the 1900 census gives George's immigration year as 1866 (not 1870), his birth as May 1835 (he would have been about 35 in 1870, not 29), and his trade was art, not farming. The City of London record is a second tested-and-rejected same-name record. See ledger Item 37.

With both candidates rejected at manifest level, the family's crossings stand as follows. George H. Bartlett's own Atlantic crossing — ship, port, and date — remains Not found: no manifest naming him has been located, and the 1866 year rests on the census entry alone. Julia's crossing (c. 1870) and Edward's crossing (c. 1872) — the years the 1900 census records for them — likewise remain Not found. The daughters' crossing stands as before, at a lower grade: the census records Julia L. and Ethel G. as immigrating in 1874, and they are identified at index level arriving at Boston that year aboard the Siberia — but that manifest page is still unread, so the Siberia identification remains index-grade only, not manifest-confirmed.

The estate under Bartlett — a studio at 218, and 220 sold off

Russell's notes add two facts that reshape the Bartlett estate. In 1898, both 218 and 220 were stables; by 1915, 218 — the carriage house — was George H. Bartlett's studio, while 220 had become a house.From Russell's notes The principal of the Normal Art School worked at home, in the carriage house across the drive — a major biographical detail for this chapter, and it means the building later fitted out as a dwelling for Florence Hunter began as the artist's own workplace. And Bartlett himself began the estate's breakup, four decades before the Hunter subdivision: in 1918 he sold parcels B and C — 220 Pleasant — to Howard A. Parker and Mollie M. Brock; in 1919 Charles A. Parker took 220 from Howard F. and Mollie M. Brock (the notes give Howard's middle initial both ways); and by 1923–24 the Gray family — Marcus J. and Ethel G. Gray — were at 220, where they remained until 1955.

The end of the era

George Bartlett died at the house in March 1923. The Arlington True List of April 1, 1923 — read from the page-image PDF — lists both Julia and Ethel G. Bartlett at 216 Pleasant, days after his death, so Julia's death is after that date; its exact date is still not found.Confirmed as to April 1, 1923 Julia, 84, and Ethel, 56, were still at 216 on April 1, 1924, and by April 1, 1925 both are gone from the list and the Hunter household is at 216 — Julia's death or removal falls in the window April 1924–April 1925; her Massachusetts death record itself is still not found, and no death date is stated.Confirmed as to the listsDeath record: Not found Russell's notes supply the disposition the probate search had not: in 1923 the George H. Bartlett estate sold parcel A — this house — to Henry H. Hunter.From Russell's notes; the deed itself not yet pulled Note the name problem the verification pass adds: the notes say "Henry H.," but every Arlington record that pass read names the man Harry H. Hunter without exception — see Chapter 3. Julia and Ethel nonetheless remain listed at 216 through 1923 and into April 1924 — the sale and the women's departure were evidently not the same event — and both are gone by April 1, 1925, when the Hunter household is listed at 216. The Middlesex Probate files for George (1923) and for Julia remain the corroborating records. The settling records for Julia: the Massachusetts death index 1923–1935 under Bartlett, Julia L. (searched in the completion pass, no entry retrieved from open indexes), the Arlington Town Clerk's death register, Mount Pleasant Cemetery's burial records, and — for the marriage — above all the GRO marriage certificate for the strong index-grade candidate found since: Newington, Dec 1857, vol. 1d, p. 347 (George Hartnell Bartlett / Julia Louisa Smith), not yet obtained; the two references the completion pass had isolated (Bermondsey 1d 103, June 1862, Julia Sherriff; Barnet 3a 185, December 1866, Julia Clark) are displaced by that earlier entry. “Smith” is now a strong candidate, not yet proven.

Chapter 3

The Hunter era, 1923–1956

In 1923, months after George Bartlett's death, his estate sold the house lot to the Hunter family — Russell's notes name the buyer Henry H. Hunter.From Russell's notes; the deed itself not yet pulled The hard-evidence pass complicates the name: every Arlington record read in that pass names him Harry H. Hunter without exception (the True Lists of 1928, 1933, 1936, 1949, and 1950), and searches under both "Henry H." and "Harry H." surfaced no draft card matching his profile — so the claim that his legal name was Henry is untested, not established, and this history calls him Harry, as the records do. He was general manager of one of Boston's great grocery stores; his wife Agatha received letters from Helen Keller. The Bartlett women stayed on into April 1924 (Julia, 84, and Ethel, 56, in the April 1, 1924 True List); by April 1, 1925 both are gone and the Hunter household is at 216 in the True List of that date Confirmed — the notes' ditto marks had covered 1924–27, and earlier research had placed the Hunters in residence only by April 1926.

The town assessors' books now bracket the transfer independently of the notes.Confirmed — assessor evidence The Assessors' Report in the Town of Arlington Annual Report 1923 (printed p. 23) assesses the 216 parcel to George H. Bartlett at $10,550; the 1924 report (printed p. 110) assesses the same parcel, at the same $10,550, to Harry H. Hunter — assessed from his 181 Cedar Ave. address. The Bartlett-to-Hunter ownership transfer therefore falls between the 1923 and 1924 assessments. And because Julia Bartlett was still the occupant in the April 1, 1924 resident list, the sequence the records give is that Hunter owned the house before he lived in it. This is assessor evidence for the transfer and its bracket; the deed itself remains unproven — it has still not been pulled (see the value table in “The value of the house” for the full 1922–1926 assessed run).

Before Pleasant Street, the Hunters lived at 181 Cedar Avenue, Arlington, by 1921, and were assessed as owners there in 1922.Confirmed Around the household at 216 in the 1920s were Thomas Forest, retired, and a live-in domestic, Mary K. Dunleavy; at the carriage house next door, from 1929, lived Florence V. Hunter.

Harry H. Hunter — and the census page that changed the search

For years the sticking point was the census: the 1950 name index failed, and the enumeration district was never determined. That is now solved. Using the Steve Morse Unified ED Finder (verified live November 22, 2026), the districts for 216 Pleasant are 1930: ED 9-169 · 1940: ED 9-26 · 1950: ED 9-38 — and the 1950 schedule itself has been read from the page image at the National Archives (ED 9-38, sheet 4, NARA image 5 of 34, line 10). One caution the page itself teaches: the Archives' AI name index reads our man as "Hunter Harris H." Only the handwriting gives "Harry H."

1950 U.S. Census — 216 Pleasant St., household 32 (ED 9-38, sheet 4, line 10)
NameHunter, Harry H. — head of household
Age / birth63 (b. ~1886/87), born in Canada (English), naturalized
Marital statusWidowed — Agatha had died before April 1950
Work48 hours a week; occupation "Proprietor," industry "Grocery," class of worker "own business"
HouseholdLiving alone — no wife, family member, or servant on his line

Three consequences follow.Confirmed as to what the schedule says (1) Harry was Canadian-born — new information that redirects the search for his origins and for the marriage record toward Canadian records, border crossings, and his draft cards; his 1942 Fourth Registration ("old man's draft") card, when pulled, will give his exact birth date and place and his employer. (2) In 1950 he was still proprietor of a grocery — consistent with the S. S. Pierce managership of 1925 having matured into a store of his own, though the schedule does not name the employer.Inference (3) On this schedule Agatha was dead by April 1950, and Harry lived alone at 216. The resident lists bracket the same interval from the other side: Agatha F. Hunter, 61, is listed at 216 on January 1, 1950, and the whole Hunter household is absent on January 1, 1951 (books read in the verification pass). But no Massachusetts death-index entry for her could be retrieved — the index is subscription/microfilm only — so the claimed 1949–1950 death window is consistent with, but not proven by, the list evidence; disappearance from a resident list is not proof of death. Her Massachusetts death record remains the single most valuable un-pulled Hunter document: it would give her maiden name, her parents, and her birthplace in one entry. (The 1950 schedule image was not re-read in the November 22 verification pass — Item 5 there — so this paragraph's census readings stand on the earlier extraction; the follow-up margin read, Item 16, has since confirmed 216 as Harry's margin address, in the page sequence 224, 220, 216, 208, 200.)

The household enumerated immediately after Harry's (dwelling 33, lines 11–15) is headed by a Donald MacJannet, 56, married, born in Massachusetts, a college administrator — and the street margin now settles where that household was. Read on November 21, 2026 from the NARA page image (ED 9-38, sheet 4, NARA image 5 of 34) and cross-checked on the FamilySearch image of the same page (ark:/61903/3:1:3QHN-PQHW-R99Q-C), the margin address beside dwelling 33 is 208 Pleasant Street.Confirmed It is not 216 and not 218. The margin sequence on that page runs 224 (Far), 220 (Gray), 216 (Harry H. Hunter, dwelling 32, line 10), 208 (MacJannet, dwelling 33), 200 (Powers) — and there is no 218 on this page. The MacJannet household at 208, lines 11–15: Donald MacJannet, 56, college administrator; his wife Chanette B., 48, born in Germany, a eurythmics teacher; two lodgers — Mrs. Frank V. Noyes, 74, widowed, and Maude Patten, 57, executive secretary; and a nephew, Klaus Blensdorf, 20, born in Germany. (This settles — and in the lodgers' names corrects — the earlier provisional extraction, which had left the dwelling's number unresolved.) He is, with high confidence, Donald Ross MacJannet (May 28, 1894 – April 4, 1986): born in Sterling, Massachusetts, son of the Scottish-born minister Robert McJannet; Tufts College 1916 (Phi Beta Kappa, French literature); founder of the MacJannet School for Young Americans at Saint-Cloud, Paris (1924) and the MacJannet Camps on Lake Annecy (1925); married Charlotte Blensdorf in 1932; and — the link that explains an Arlington address — in 1944 he established a Vacation School of French with Tufts College located in Arlington, and his Tufts work matches the schedule's "college administrator." His papers are the Donald and Charlotte MacJannet Papers (MS024) at the Tufts Archival Research Center, and his biography is Schoolmaster of Kings (Herbert Jacobs, 1982).Strong inference on identity The completion pass tested the school's address against Tufts' own sources: the Tufts Archival Research Center biography (MS024, tarc.tufts.edu) says, in its exact wording: “In 1944, they established the Vacation School of French with Tufts College. Located in Arlington, MA, the purpose of the summer school was to educate people in French language and culture so that they might take up rehabilitation work in post-war France.” Russell Miller's Light on the Hill: A History of Tufts College, 1852–1952 corroborates: “In the summer of 1944 it co-sponsored, with Mr. and Mrs. Donald R. MacJannet, a six-weeks ‘Vacation School of French,’ the theme of which was training for rehabilitation work in war-torn France.” No Tufts or archival source read in that pass states a street address for the school.School address unverified The Tufts exhibit “The MacJannet Legacy” lists among its items a “Tufts College Vacation School of French brochure, 1948” — the brochure itself was not opened/read in that pass and is the named next source for the school itself. The census result confirms the verified prior from the lists: in the January 1, 1949, January 1, 1950, and January 1, 1951 Arlington lists the MacJannets' address is 208 Pleasant Street — and the follow-up read extends the run: still at 208 on January 1, 1953, with age and occupation shown as dashes, and gone from 208 by January 1, 1954. Census and town lists agree on 208; there is no discrepancy to explain. For the school, the consequence is one of labelling: any claim that the Vacation School of French was at 216 or 218 is Unproven — unsupported by the census and the town lists, both of which place the MacJannets' home at 208.

Both schedules have since been read from the page images — the 1940 sheet in an earlier pass and the 1930 sheet on November 22, 2026 (the two sections that follow). The 1930 page shows Harry, Agatha, their daughter Joan at 6, Agatha's father Thomas Forrest, and the servant Mary Dunleavy at 216, and Florence's household at 218 — and it answers the census's famous "radio set" question for both houses: each had a set. The bracket on the tenure itself has now been settled by the books themselves — against Russell's notes for 1951, and for them in 1952–53. The notes place Harry, with Geraldine M. Hunter, in the 216 household in the resident lists of 1951, 1952, and 1953. The verification pass read the January 1, 1951 list (printed p. 77) and searched the whole volume: there is no entry for 216 Pleasant in 1951, and no Harry, Agatha, or Geraldine Hunter anywhere in the book — the claim that Geraldine M. Hunter appears at 216 in 1951 is refuted.Refuted by the record itself (Caveat carried from the pass: the 1951 finding rests on the book's page-image-derived text layer for p. 77 plus whole-book search-inside; the rendered page image itself was still loading during the live check.) The Hunter household's presence in the lists therefore breaks after January 1, 1950 — but it resumes. A follow-up read of the next three books (Archive.org page images; printed pp. 79, 79, and 78) shows Harry back at 216, with Geraldine, on January 1, 1952, January 1, 1953, and January 1, 1954Confirmed — so the notes' run stands for 1952 and 1953 and is refuted only for 1951. Whether Harry actually moved out during 1950 and returned, or was simply missed by the 1951 list, the books do not say. He retained title throughout: he was still conveying the estate's lots in 1954–56 (next section).

The 1930 census — the household in full, and a relationship settled

The 1930 schedule has now been read from the page image.Confirmed 1930 U.S. Census, Arlington, ED 9-169, Sheet 10B (NARA T626 roll 914; Archive.org massachusettscensus00reel914), enumerated April 12, 1930; the page image is archived in the project archive (read November 22, 2026; MD5 7f8b3851171ed5abf385b56fb11372e1). It is the fullest single snapshot of the Hunter household at 216 — and it settles the Forest question outright. The sheet covers both houses of the old estate:

1930 U.S. Census — 216 Pleasant St. (ED 9-169, Sheet 10B, dwelling 206, family 232, enumerated April 12, 1930)
Harry H. Hunter43, head of household — born Canada-English, immigrated 1899, naturalized; home owned, valued at $10,000 as first written, overwritten to read $60,000 — a disputed reading (the value entry, line 58, is heavily overwritten; both readings are published, neither alone); radio set; occupation manager of a groceries company.
Agatha Hunter40, wife — born Canada-English, immigrated 1905. Flagged, not settled: her middle initial on this schedule appears to read “D.” — against T (seen on the 1928 page image), F, and P in the Arlington resident lists; the initial remains unusable as a search key.
Joan Hunter6, daughter — born in Massachusetts, in school. Her earliest appearance in any record read for this history — a decade before the 1940 sheet that first documented her (below).

1930 U.S. Census — 218 Pleasant St. (same sheet)
Florence V. Hunter69, living alone — renting at $75 a month, with a radio set. Flagged, not settled: her marital status is written “M” on this schedule, though the 1940 census (below) records her as widowed.

What the sheet settles.Confirmed as to what the schedule says (1) Thomas Forrest was Agatha's father. The schedule enters him in the relationship column as Harry's father-in-law — the Forest hypothesis, carried as Unproven elsewhere in this history on the strength of his presence in the household, is settled by the record itself: he was Agatha's father, and her maiden name follows as Forrest, in the schedule's spelling. (2) Joan in 1930. Joan Hunter is at 216 aged 6, in school — consistent with the 16-year-old of the 1940 sheet and the Arlington High School Class of 1941. (3) Dunleavy in 1930. Mary Dunleavy is still the household's servant in April 1930, with her birthplace (Irish Free State) and immigration year (1920) now on the record — squarely inside her resident-list bracket, which closes with her absence from the April 1, 1931 list. (4) Florence renting. At 218 Florence is a renter at $75 a month in 1930; by 1940 she owns her house (valued at $9,000, next section) — the two schedules bracket a purchase in between, though no deed for it has been read.Inference (5) The sheet's edges. No household at 212 or 214 appears on the sheet — the enumerator passes from 216 directly to 208. And both houses of the estate had a radio set in 1930 — the household context for the brass “RADIO” outlet that survives in the house itself (Chapter 3 · II). See ledger Item 3, now closed.

The 1940 census — a daughter appears

The 1940 schedule has now been read from the page image.Confirmed 1940 U.S. Census, Arlington, ED 9-26, Sheet 11A (NARA Catalog NAID 126377073, T627 Roll 1601), enumerated April 22, 1940; the source image is archived in the project archive as census/1940-ed9-26-sheet11a.jpg. The sheet covers both houses of the old estate:

Three things the sheet settles.Confirmed as to what the schedule says (1) Joan Hunter. Harry and Agatha had a daughter at home in 1940 — Joan, 16, Massachusetts-born, highest grade completed H-2 (line 38) — who appears in no resident list, deed, or other record read for this history before this page; she is new to the household's documented membership. Her name is Joan, not Jean: a re-read of the page image (November 22, 2026) shows the enumerator wrote “Joan,” and the earlier “Jean” was a misreading of the handwriting.Confirmed A second primary record now documents her in her own right: the Arlington High School yearbook, Class of 1941, printed p. 41, gives her senior entry, with her portrait — “JOAN HUNTER, 216 Pleasant Street, Ski Club, Riding Club — Interesting Joan agrees that there is nothing like sailing. She'll never forget her Fine Arts class… Jackson is the college for her.” Her AHS class of 1941 and her stated intention to attend Jackson College are Confirmed. A third primary record now shows she went: the Tufts Jumbo yearbook of 1942, student directory, “Class of 1945—Jackson” section (printed p. 181), lists “JOAN HUNTER, Alpha Xi Delta — 216 Pleasant Street, Arlington, Mass.” — her attendance at Jackson College (Tufts) is Confirmed. Her graduation is now settled as a verified negative through June 1947: she did not receive a Jackson College degree at any of Tufts' three 1944–45 degree ceremonies — the Jackson College candidate lists were read in full in the official Tufts Commencement Office programs for the Degree Convocation of October 22, 1944, the Degree Convocation of February 18, 1945, and the 89th Annual Commencement of June 17, 1945 (all three programs archived in the project archive from the Tufts Digital Library), and her name appears in none of them. The previously missing ceremony has now also been read: the Degree Convocation of October 21, 1945 (Tufts Digital Library record jq086051m), whose Jackson College lists — BA: Bedworth, Bowles, Fitzpatrick, Gaffny, Hogan, Hunt, Lane; BS: Fowler; BS in Chemistry: Carter, Hawes — contain no Hunter. And the Tufts Ninety-first Annual Commencement program of June 15, 1947 (Tufts Digital Library, archived) has now been read from the page image: Joan Hunter appears in none of its Jackson College degree lists, and its “degrees awarded subsequent” section names only two dental graduates. She therefore took no Jackson degree — every Tufts degree ceremony from October 1944 through June 1947 has now been read, and she appears in none of them Confirmed. She left Tufts without graduating Confirmed. Her birth record, her marriage, and her later life remain Not found — still being researched, and nothing further about her is stated in this history. See ledger Items 23–25. (2) Florence in 1940. At 218, Florence V. Hunter was 79, widowed and living alone in a house she owned, valued at $9,000, born Canada-English, and in the same house in 1935 — a decade into her carriage-house tenure, and consistent with the True Lists that place her at 218 in 1936 and 1949. (3) Who is not there. No Thomas Forest and no Mary K. Dunleavy appears at either address in 1940 — consistent with the lists, which last show Forest in 1933 and Dunleavy in 1928, and with neither reappearing at 216 in any later record read. Harry's entry also carries the limit of the page itself: his 1939 wage entry is smudged and illegible in the image, so this history states no wage figure for him. See ledger Item 17.

Harry after 1950 — the subdivider, and two new Hunters

The registry rewrites the end of Harry's story. He was alive and conveying land through February 14, 1956: as grantor, with M. Geraldine Hunter, he sold Pleasant Street lots to Archie N. and Christine MacDonald on May 7, 1954 (Book 8250, Page 305) and to Robert M. and Leona Weiss Brownell on January 16, 1956 (Book 8652, Page 134), with two further deeds on May 28, 1954 and February 14, 1956 whose details were not opened.Confirmed — MassLandRecords, read live So Harry himself, not a developer, subdivided the estate in 1954–56 (see Chapter 4), and his death is after February 14, 1956 — the resident lists show the household absent on January 1, 1951 but back at 216, with Geraldine, on January 1, 1952, 1953, and 1954, so he was living in the house again in the subdivision years while retaining title.Inference His death date, place, and burial after 1956 are still not found;Not found the 1955, 1956, and 1957 True Lists, read in the follow-up pass, confirm he does not reappear anywhere in Arlington in those years — where he and Geraldine went after leaving 216 in 1954 remains Unproven / open. The highest-value single record is his September 1918 WWI draft registration card (exact birth date, birthplace, nearest relative), with the St. Albans border-crossing lists, his naturalization petition (NARA Boston), the 1901/1911 Canadian censuses, the Massachusetts death index 1956–1970, his Middlesex probate file, and Mount Pleasant Cemetery as the rest of the route.

The completion pass searched the Hunter vital records directly and retrieved none of them from open indexes — each negative is stated with its coverage so it can be audited. Barry H. Hunter's birth: no candidate found. General-index searches for a Massachusetts birth of Barry Hunter (and Barry as middle name) to Harry/Henry Hunter and Agatha, c. 1910–1932, returned no birth index entry or record; Massachusetts birth records of that era are not fully open online, so the negative is from open web indexes only, not from the Massachusetts Archives index volumes. Agatha's maiden name therefore remains unknown from this route.Not found Geraldine's marriage: not found. No index entry for a marriage of Henry H. Hunter or Harry H. Hunter to a Geraldine (any surname) in 1949–1955 was retrieved from any open index; whether M. Geraldine Hunter was Harry's second wife remains untested by a marriage record.Not found Harry/Henry's death: not found. FamilySearch SSDI searches, verified live, returned 0 results for Harry Hunter, b. 1885–1889, death place Massachusetts, and for Henry Hunter, b. 1885–1889 (no place filter). Caveat carried from the pass: SSDI coverage is thin before 1962, so a 1956–1961 death could be missed. No Massachusetts death-index entry 1956–1975 under either name was retrieved. Name-in-use evidence: Brookline Directory 1925 — “Hunter Harry H gen mgr 1324 Beacon h at Arlington,” with “PIERCE S S COMPANY Grocers 1324 Beacon Coolidge Corner” (LDSGenealogy AI-OCR transcription of the archive.org scan; verify against the scan before quoting). This supports “Harry H.” as the name in use; the “Henry H.” legal-name claim remains Unproven. A further same-name rejection from the pass: Henry H. Hunter, Baltimore National Cemetery (b. 11/06/1914, d. 06/11/1951, PFC, Korea) — wrong generation.

Two new people step out of those deeds — and Russell's notes now dispute one of them. The registry's name index reads the June 30, 1954 deed of the 216 house lot (Book 8280, Page 600) as granted by Barry H. Hunter, with M. Geraldine Hunter, to Helen S. Brine. Russell's notes say flatly: "Henry H. and Geraldine Hunter sold B (216) to Helen S. Brine." One of the two readings is wrong, and the deed image itself — not the index, not the notes — settles whether the grantor was Henry or Barry.Open conflict If Henry, Barry H. Hunter's role shrinks to the other 1954–56 deeds and the index reading was wrong; if Barry, the notes misattribute the sale. On the index reading, Barry is otherwise a ghost: that deed is his only Middlesex South record, and nothing else about him was found on the open web; the natural reading would be Harry's son and heir, holding the house lot jointly with Geraldine while Harry sold the out-lots.Inference M. Geraldine Hunter co-granted with Harry (1954, 1956) and, on one reading or the other, with Barry or beside Harry on the house-lot deed (1954). Russell's notes place her in the 216 household in the resident lists of 1951, 1952, and 1953 — the 1951 book itself refutes that for 1951 (no 216 entry, and no Geraldine Hunter anywhere in the volume), but the follow-up read of the 1952, 1953, and 1954 books confirms her at 216 in all three years, as Harry's fellow householder (the entries are tabulated below). Her residence at 216 is therefore established for 1952–54Confirmed; the deeds add her role as co-grantor in the registry. The reading that she was Harry's second wife after Agatha (a wife co-grants to release homestead) remains possible but unproven; the alternative remains that she was Barry's wife holding jointly with both men.Unproven The settling records: Harry's Middlesex probate file (which would name his heirs), the Massachusetts marriage index c. 1950–54 for a Hunter remarriage, Barry's Massachusetts birth record — which, if he was Agatha's son, would name her maiden name directly — and the recitals in the deed images themselves.

The follow-up read of the next three books closes the Hunter residence story. In the January 1, 1955 list (printed p. 79) neither Harry nor Geraldine appears at 216 — or anywhere else in the volume — and they are likewise absent from the 1956 and 1957 books: having been at 216 on January 1, 1954, they left during calendar 1954, the year the house lot went to Helen S. Hunter born June 6, 1893, with an Indiana Social Security number, who died in 1981. The verification pass adds two more explicit rejections from its draft-card searches: Harry H. Hunter; the underlying draft indexes are interactive or subscription-gated, so this is "not found," not "does not exist."Not found

Agatha, and the Forest hypothesis

Agatha Hunter (b. ~1888/89) is the household's most vivid figure and its least documented. What the books themselves establish, from the verification pass: she is at 216 in the True Lists of 1928 (39, housewife), 1933 (44, housewife), 1936 (47, at home), 1940 (51, housewife), 1941 (52, housewife), 1942 (age printed 63 — an anomaly against 52 the year before; flagged as printed, not harmonized), 1943 (54, at home — back in sequence), 1944 (55, at home), 1945 (56, at home), 1946 (57, housewife), 1947 (58, at home), 1948 (59, housewife), 1949 (60, housewife), and January 1, 1950 (61, housewife). One gap in that run is the book's, not the family's: the 1938 street page (printed p. 16, Precinct 6) has no entry for 216 at all — a probable omission by the book, as happened again in 1951 — since the Hunters are proven at 216 in the 1939 list and the April 1940 census.Inference — probable book omission And the whole Hunter household is absent on January 1, 1951. Harry is widowed on the April 1950 census schedule (earlier extraction). No Massachusetts death-index entry for her could be retrieved in the pass — the Massachusetts Death Index, 1901–1980, is subscription/microfilm only, and no entry could be read under Agatha Hunter or under Agatha P., Agatha F., or Agatha S. Hunter, in either the claimed 1949–1950 window or the widened 1945–1950 window. So the 1949–1950 death window is consistent with, but not proven by, the list evidence, and her death date remains not found.Not found Her middle initial is ruined as a search key — and the pass shows the disagreement is inside the books themselves: the only letterform actually seen on a page image is T (1928 street section, printed p. 212 — flat top bar, vertical stem from the center, no mid-height cross-stroke; the book's OCR of that page also reads "T"), while the same volume's alphabetical section is OCR'd "F," the 1933 text layer reads F, the 1936 text layer reads P, and the 1949–1951 books read F. The 1933 and 1936 letterforms rest on the books' OCR text layers, not page images — drop the initial entirely as a search key. (Russell's notes give still other initials and place her in every list through 1949, missing only in 1938 — notes-only detail, not tested against those years' books.) In the 1920s–30s the household included Thomas Forest, retired. The hypothesis — that Forest was Agatha's father, and her maiden name therefore Forest — was reasonable and untested when the pass ran; the 1930 census has since settled it (see “The 1930 census” above): Thomas Forrest is entered there as Harry's father-in-law — Agatha's father — with the surname spelled “Forrest” on the schedule.Confirmed — relationship The pass confirms Forest's arc from the books: present in 1928 (73, retired — page image) and present in 1933 (81, at home — text layer) and in 1934 (82 — page image), absent in 1935 — and from the whole 1935 book — so he died or departed between April 1, 1934 and April 1, 1935, which narrows his death-record search to that single year. His two ages imply birth about 1854/55 versus about 1851/52 — a minor internal inconsistency between the lists, noted. Harry's Canadian birth, revealed by the 1950 schedule, does not touch Agatha's origins either way. The settling records: the Hunter marriage record, c. 1908–1915 (Massachusetts index — and now Canadian indexes too), which names her maiden name and parents; Thomas Forest's Massachusetts death record, c. 1934–1935; and above all Agatha's own death record.

S. S. Pierce and the Coolidge Corner store

In 1925 Harry Hunter was general manager of the S. S. Pierce Co. store at 1324 Beacon Street, Coolidge Corner, Brookline (Brookline Directory, 1925).Confirmed It was a substantial white-collar post. S. S. Pierce, founded in 1831 by Samuel Stillman Pierce (1807–1880) with Eldad Worcester as a wholesale provisions firm supplying ships' captains, had become Boston's carriage-trade grocer: a Copley Square store from 1887, and at Coolidge Corner the Tudor-style clock-tower building of 1898–99 (Winslow and Wetherell), built after Wallace Pierce bought the former Coolidge & Brother store on the site in 1892. The tower was damaged in the 1944 hurricane (one source says a 1948 storm — the discrepancy is flagged, not resolved) and rebuilt without its open belvedere. The firm was sold to Seneca Foods in 1972; the name survived into the 1980s. The man at 216 ran one of the great food stores of greater Boston into the Depression; his 1950 self-description as a grocery "proprietor" suggests he ended his career running a store of his own or as proprietor-manager.Inference

One more lead, handled carefully: a "Harry H. Hunter" appears as a customer in Historic New England's Irving & Casson–A. H. Davenport 1925 sales journal. A furniture purchase in 1925 would fit the Hunters' 1924–26 move beautifully — but fit is not proof, and the identity is unconfirmed.Unproven The journal page's full entry (does it give an address?) at Historic New England's archives would settle it.

Chapter 3 · II

The Helen Keller letters

Helen Keller wrote to Agatha Hunter personally — once beyond reasonable doubt, in 1932, and probably three times in all; each letter below is weighed on its own evidence. The letters are social, not institutional: thanks for boxes of sweets and a Thanksgiving basket, news of illness and lost dogs. Both surviving originals are now in anonymous private hands; what the public record holds is the auction listings, and the photographs below.

How we know the recipient is this Agatha

The chain has three links. (1) RR Auction describes the 1932 letter as a "Letter to Agatha Hunter in Arlington, Massachusetts," and it sold with its original mailing envelope — the identification almost certainly comes off the envelope itself. (2) Arlington had exactly one Agatha Hunter: the town's resident lists put Harry H. Hunter's wife Agatha at 216 Pleasant in 1926, 1929, and 1939 in the earlier research, and the books read in the verification pass put her there in 1928, 1933, 1936, 1949, and on January 1, 1950, and no other Agatha Hunter appears in them; the letter's date, March 1932, falls squarely inside that tenure. The only other Hunter household in town was a different Harry, at 62 Amsden Street, whose wife was Josephine. (3) The identification is strong but not absolute proof — it leans on the auction house's reading of an envelope now in the buyer's hands.Strong identification

Letter one — November 27, 1923

A typed letter, one page both sides, to "Mrs. Harry Hunter," thanking her for "the daintiest box of sweets," mentioning Polly Thomson's return and "Teacher" — Anne Sullivan — wanting an Irish setter puppy, with a joke about Prohibition. It sold at RR Auction (#622) on December 8, 2021, for $491.25. If the recipient is Agatha,Unproven but plausible the acquaintance predates the move to 216 — the Hunters were then at 181 Cedar Avenue — and was already warm by 1923. RR Auction lot listing

Letter two — March 9, 1932

Three pages, written from The Homestead, Hot Springs, Virginia, to Agatha at Arlington; sold at RR Auction (lot 310) on November 10, 2021, for $777.50, with its original envelope, the return address in Polly Thomson's hand. Keller opens with an apology for her "graceless silence" since hearing of Agatha's illness while Keller was on holiday in Brittany the summer before, and for never thanking her for a Christmas box of sweets. Then the household's grim Christmas, in the published excerpts: Polly Thomson was in the hospital recovering from an appendectomy; Anne Sullivan could not see well enough to read or shop; and both their dogs went missing — Darky the Scotch terrier for four days, Helga the Great Dane for eight. By January Polly had recovered, the dogs were found, and the two were back on the road, "going from one meeting to another for the blind." Whatever fills the rest of the third page was never transcribed — RR Auction printed only excerpts ("in part"), so no complete public transcription of this letter exists. RR Auction lot 310

Letter three — the Thanksgiving basket (undated)

One page, to "Mrs. H. Hunter," thanking her for a Thanksgiving gift basket; sold at RR Auction (lot 316) on January 12, 2022, for $723. On its wording alone this one could belong to either Arlington Mrs. H. Hunter; what ties it to Agatha is provenance — it surfaced at the same auction house two months after the Agatha letter, which fits one consignor dispersing one woman's Keller correspondence.Attribution probable, not proven The lot included its envelope, addressed in Polly Thomson's hand — the buyer holds the one thing that would settle it. The letter itself is a small comic play in three voices, as the household opened the basket:

"What a wonderful basket! It filled our little house with brightness and cheer… If you could have been concealed in the draperies or in the sun-parlor, you would have been amused to hear the three of us express, each in her own way, her delight over the basket."

Polly the Hospitable. Of course we must have a party right off while we have these good things.
Helen the Greedy. Why a party? Can't we eat them all ourselves?
Mrs. Macy the Experienced. Most of these things will keep indefinitely, you know.

— Helen Keller to Mrs. H. Hunter, undated; "Mrs. Macy" is Anne Sullivan Macy. Full page pictured below. RR Auction lot 316

Who has the letters now?

Nobody knows, publicly. RR Auction sold the 1932 letter on November 10, 2021 and the Thanksgiving letter on January 12, 2022, and auction houses do not name their buyers; neither letter has resurfaced since, so both are presumably in a private autograph collection. Two Keller letters to the same woman surfacing at the same house two months apart suggests a single consignor dispersing her Keller correspondence — possibly out of an estate. That owner is anonymous too. Keller's office often kept copies of her outgoing mail, so the archive route below remains the one place a copy might still turn up.

How did Agatha know Helen Keller?

Not found.Not found The letters are personal — gift boxes of sweets, a gift basket — which places the Hunters in Keller's personal gift-exchange circle between 1923 and 1932, and the recurring gifts run through the grocery trade's gift economy as plausibly as through any institution: a grocer's wife sends hampers. Whether the connection was Perkins School for the Blind (Keller's Massachusetts base, in Watertown and South Boston), the American Foundation for the Blind (her employer from 1924, for 44 years; she bequeathed her papers to it), or a mutual friend is unknown. The archive search has now been partly run: the Perkins School Archives' Helen Keller ephemera collection (AG160) lists no Hunter item in its Series 5 correspondence container list, and none of the three RR Auction lots states a consignor or any provenance. The AFB's Helen Keller Archive (160,000+ artifacts, afb.org/HelenKellerArchive) has not yet been searched internally for "Agatha Hunter" — that search, a direct query to the Perkins archivist, and the Helen Keller Papers at the Schlesinger Library remain the named routes. Any Hunter letters there would be book-grade primary material.

The household through the Depression and the war — and a brass outlet

The Hunters' Arlington was booming around them: the town grew 93% in the 1920s (18,665 in 1920 to 36,094 in 1930) and reached 40,013 in 1940 and 44,353 in 1950 — a streetcar suburb turning into an automobile suburb. Household specifics for the 1930s and the war years waited on the 1940 schedule (ED 9-26) — which has now been read (Chapter 3, ledger Item 17): it shows Harry still manager of a retail grocery in 1940, Agatha beside him, and their daughter Joan, 16, at home and in school; Harry's 1939 wage entry on that page is smudged and illegible, so his income from that source remains unstated.Confirmed

One artifact survives in the house itself: a brass "RADIO" antenna/ground outlet, most likely installed 1928–1935, presumably by the Hunters.Inference from the object's type and the tenure Boston was an early radio city (WBZ from 1921; WNAC and WEEI followed), and wiring a dedicated aerial-and-ground outlet into the parlor wall was what a prosperous household did for the new medium. The 1930 census famously asked every household whether it owned a "radio set" — the Hunter household's answer sits on the unpulled ED 9-169 schedule, a direct documentary tie between the census page and the brass plate on the wall.

Chapter 4

The Brine years, 1951–1981

The "lost decades" are lost no longer — at least in outline. The deed chain, read live on MassLandRecords (Middlesex South) in November 2026, shows the Hunter family itself breaking up the estate in 1954–56, and a single owner, Helen S. Brine, holding the house for the next 27 years. The True Lists now name who lived in the house continuously from 1955 through January 1, 1981 — the last list year of Brine's ownership, in which she is still listed at 216, with only Keith A. Larson remaining of her household; her departure falls between that list and her June 8, 1981 deed to the Russells, and the January 1, 1982 list closes the run: Brine is gone, Robert Mitchell and Sharon Stanton Russell are in place at 216, and Larson has stayed on. The January 1, 1983 list carries the Russell household a year further — Larson still staying on, with a new resident, Gettner Shormeen, beside the Russells — and the January 1, 1984 list holds the household at the Russells and Larson, Shormeen by then gone, and the January 1, 1985 list brings Sharmeen back — spelled “Sharmeen” in 1985 against “Shormeen” in 1983 — with Larson now printed as Student against Edit/Res in 1975–1984. No True List year for the Brine era remains unread. The 1993 list has since been read ahead of the intervening years: the same four residents continue at 216 — Keith A. Larson, Brooke Alden Russell, and Robert Mitchell and Sharon Stanton Russell — with the book's own precinct placement of the household flagged, not harmonized, below. The 1997 list — now titled the “1997 Street Listing,” printing year of birth instead of age — has since been read ahead of the intervening years as well: only three residents remain at 216 — Keith A. Larson (b. 1941, Editor), Robert Mitchell Russell (b. 1941, Physician), and Sharon Stanton Russell (b. 1944, Planner) — and Brooke Alden Russell, at 216 in the lists from 1988 through 1996, is gone and appears nowhere in the book. The 1999 list — the “1999 Street Listing,” still printing year of birth — has since been read as well: the same three remain at 216 — Keith A. Larson (b. 1941, now printed “Edit Dept”), Robert Mitchell Russell (b. 1941, Physician), and Sharon Stanton Russell (b. 1944, Planner) — with no resident change at any estate address from the 1998 list; the remaining open list years are the Russell era, 1986–1992 and 1994–1996.

The Hunters subdivide their own estate

The bracket the earlier research established — parcels connected until "the early 1950s," the 1927 Sanborn atlas (updated to February 1951) showing the estate intact and a 1973 Sanborn showing it divided — now has names and dates inside it. Harry H. Hunter, with M. Geraldine Hunter, sold Pleasant Street lots to the MacDonalds (May 7, 1954) and the Brownells (January 16, 1956); the house lot — "Lot B," 216 itself — went to Helen S. Brine on June 30, 1954, granted by M. Geraldine Hunter with a second Hunter the registry's name index reads as Barry H. and Russell's notes read as Henry H. (the dispute is laid out in Chapter 3).Confirmed as to the sale — MassLandRecords; grantor in dispute The subdivider the six-owner test was looking for was not an outside developer: it was the Hunter family. Russell's notes corroborate the registry from the other side — they record the same 1953 re-lettering of the estate ("A1 and A2 became B, C, D, E, F"), the same Brownell purchase (1956) and the Macdonalds at 214 (spelled "Macdonald" in the lists), and the same 1954 sale of lot B to Brine, with Helen Brine then selling B to R. Russell in 1981. One earlier candidate stays eliminated: Frank L. Newcomb, whose name surfaces near the Hunters' spot in a 1952 resident list, has a clean separate trail as a hardware estimator across town through 1955 — the sighting was most likely a quirk of how the list is ordered.

Helen S. Brine, 1954–1981

Helen S. Brine owned 216 Pleasant from June 30, 1954 until June 8, 1981 — 27 years, the house's second-longest tenure after the Bartletts'.Confirmed as owner (Russell's handwritten summary says "24 yrs" for 1954–1981; the span is 27 calendar years, and the handwritten figure should not be repeated.) Almost everything else about her is not found:Not found web searches returned only unrelated Helen Brines, all rejected. Russell's notes gave her a household for the first years — in 1954 the names at 216 are "Scammell, Brine, Frost"; in 1955, "Brine, Frances S., Brine, Helen S., Frost, Scammer" [Scammell]; in 1956, "Brine, Helen S., Frost, Scammell" — and the follow-up read of the True List books themselves (Archive.org page images) now confirms and fills out that household.Confirmed On January 1, 1955 (printed p. 79), six people are at 216, every one with their 1954 residence given as Somerville: Frances S. Brine, 89, retired; Helen S. Brine, 64, personnel; Frances M. Frost, 69, teacher; Frank H. Scammell, 22, student; Henry Scammell, 21, investigator; and Madeline B. Scammell, 56, teacher. The same six are at 216 on January 1, 1956 (printed p. 78). On January 1, 1957 (printed p. 79) only four remain: Helen S. Brine, 66, retired; Frances M. Frost, 71; Frank H. Scammell, 24, engineer; and Madeleine Scammell, 58, teacher — Frances S. Brine and Henry Scammell are gone. Whether Frances S. Brine, 89 in 1955, died in 1956 is Unproven / open — disappearance from a resident list is not proof of death. The lists give no relationships among the six, and none is stated here: how the Brines, Frost, and Scammells were connected, if at all, the books do not say. One registry detail hints at Helen's end: the municipal-lien certificate recorded the same day as the 1981 sale names "BRINE HELEN S EST" — suggesting she died shortly before the sale and her estate conveyed the house.Inference The completion pass searched for her independently and did not identify her from any record read: searches of the web index for Helen S. Brine of Arlington / 216 Pleasant, and FamilySearch SSDI searches (Helen Brine, death 1980–1982, Massachusetts; and Helen Brine, all years) returned 0 results (verified live). No census schedule (1900–1950), Massachusetts index entry, or maiden name was obtained in that pass. The only facts it could state were the deed premises themselves (owner 1954–1981; “BRINE HELEN S EST” on the June 8, 1981 lien certificate), which it could not corroborate from an independent record.Not found in open indexes The follow-up read of the 1955–1957 True Lists has since supplied the first independent record of her: Helen S. Brine at 216, aged 64 with occupation "personnel" in 1955 and 66, retired, in 1957 — and Frances S. Brine is now identified at least as a fellow resident of 216 in 1955–56, aged 89 and retired, though nothing further about her was read. The settling records for her life remain: her Middlesex South Probate file (c. 1981), which would give her death date, heirs, and history, and the Massachusetts death index c. 1980–81. The Arlington True Lists have since been read for her household year by year through January 1, 1981, and the January 1, 1982 list closes the run — Brine gone, the Russells in place, Keith A. Larson stayed on (see the household sections below and ledger Items 39, 42, 43, 44, and 45); no True List year for the Brine era remains unread.
