What those owners left behind is legible in the house itself: when the National Register surveyors came in 1985, mid-Brine-to-Russell transition, they recorded major alterations "None" and outbuildings "None." Whoever held 216 for those decades, they did not remodel it out of its Greek Revival self.

Chapter 5

The Russells

In June 1981 the house passed from Helen Brine's estate years to a scholar of international migration and her husband, for $170,000 — and in November 2015 it passed from them, for $1 million, to its sixth owners.

Sharon Stanton Russell (1944–2013)

Sharon Stanton Russell died on February 27, 2013, age 68, of Arlington, after a prolonged illness (Boston Globe obituary, published March 9–10, 2013).Confirmed Born in 1944 in Oceanside, New York, she took a BA at Wellesley College (1966), an MA at the University of Chicago (1974), an MPA at the Harvard Kennedy School (1982), and a PhD at MIT in 1987 (Political Science), under Myron Weiner. She was a Senior Research Scholar at MIT's Center for International Studies, where she long directed the Inter-University Committee on International Migration (IUCIM) and the Mellon-MIT Program on NGOs and Forced Migration — a pioneering scholar of international migration: global trends, migration and development, forced migration; an adviser to the United Nations and the World Bank, a member of two UN Expert Groups, and on the Academic Advisory Board of the International Organization for Migration. Her dissertation is now identified from the MIT DSpace record itself: Uneasy welcome — the political economy in migration policy in Kuwait, PhD, MIT Department of Political Science, 1987, advisor Myron Weiner.Confirmed — MIT DSpace The DSpace record ( hdl.handle.net/1721.1/111071 ) gives the exact title as “Uneasy welcome--the political economy in migration policy in Kuwait,” author “Russell, Sharon Stanton, 1944–,” publisher Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and the description “Thesis (Ph. D.)--Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Dept. of Political Science, 1987. Bibliography: v. 2, leaves 396-422.” No abstract appears on the DSpace record as read, and no ProQuest abstract was retrieved in the November 2026 completion pass.Abstract not found A discrepancy is flagged, not harmonised: the account that she took a Harvard Kennedy MPA in 1982 conflicts with her Globe/Legacy obituary as indexed, which says MA 1982 at Harvard's Kennedy School of Government. The MIT Reports to the President 2013–2014, Center for International Studies section, memorialised her as a longtime colleague who “earned her PhD at MIT under the late Myron Weiner, was director of the InterUniversity Committee on International Migration, hosted by CIS, for many years and was a leading migration scholar.” Her memorial service was held March 23, 2013, at Annisquam Village Church, Gloucester. She was survived by her husband, Robert Mitchell Russell, daughters Kimberley Russell Slate and Brooke Russell, and sisters Diana Stanton-Thornbrough and Pamela Stanton (obituary). Globe obituary

Publications — a partial checklist

  • International Migration and Development in Sub-Saharan Africa, Vols. I–II (World Bank Discussion Papers 101–102, 1990; with Karen Jacobsen).
  • International Migration and International Trade (World Bank, 1992; with Michael S. Teitelbaum).
  • Contributor, International Migration Systems: A Global Approach (Oxford, 1992).
  • "International Migration: Global Trends and National Responses," Fletcher Forum of World Affairs 20:2 (1996).
  • Co-editor, with Myron Weiner, Demography and National Security (Berghahn, 2001).
  • Contributor, Beyond Six Billion (National Academies, 2000); a remittances-model article in International Migration Review (1986); co-PI on a Harvard Weatherhead project on the 1947 Partition of India (2005–06).

Robert Mitchell Russell — "Rob Russell," confirmed

The question is closed. The November 3, 2015 deed (Book 66331, Page 188) names the grantor as Robert Mitchell Russell, trustee of the Russell Family Arlington Nominee Trust, conveying 216 Pleasant to Matthew Dawson and Chia-Yun Sun for $1,000,000 — and Sharon's obituary names Robert Mitchell Russell as her husband. Rob Russell, the current owner's friend who sold them the house, is Robert Mitchell Russell.Confirmed by the deed He and Sharon bought the house together from Helen S. Brine on June 8, 1981, for $170,000 (Book 14312, Page 236). Arlington Historic District Commission minutes style the property "Russell" through 2014 — including a certificate-of-appropriateness file for a soffit vent ("216 Pleasant St. (Russell – 13-63P – Bush – COA (soffit vent)," minutes of September 18 and November 20, 2014) — and the September 2014 minutes carry an item, "Call re: Pleasant Street property currently on real estate market," consistent with a 2014–15 listing.Confirmed Robert Mitchell Russell's own occupation and background beyond the obituary and the deeds were not found in public web sources.Not found (Living person — public records only.)

Rob Russell's own research

In November 2026, Rob Russell passed the current owners his own research on the estate: four typed pages headed "216, 218, 220 — Swan-Gage-Bartlett estate," a year-by-year title and occupancy chronology running from 1852 to 2007, drawn from deeds and Arlington resident lists, with a handwritten tenure summary in the margin of the last page. It arrived second-hand, as his recollection and compilation — not as records themselves — and this history treats it that way: flagged wherever it stands alone, and checked against the registry wherever the two overlap (they agree on the Brine purchase, the 1953 re-lettering of the parcels, and the Brownell and Macdonald sales). The full transcription, with photographs of the pages, is the next section.

The 2015 sale and the present owners

The house sold on November 3, 2015, for $1,000,000 (deed Book 66331, Page 188; property records: 4,180 sq ft, 0.273 acre).Confirmed The buyers were Matt Dawson and Chia Yun Sun. Their documented stewardship, from public filings only: the March 26, 2023 letter to the Arlington ZBA opposing a special permit for a large addition at 212 Pleasant Street — the letter that supplies the six-owner statement, the estate history, the pond easement, and the Henry Call ice-documentary lead, and that describes nearly eight years of residence, kayaking and skating on Spy Pond, and the easement as "one of the main reasons we live here." The 212 case (applicant Nellie Aikenhead; a proposal to grow a nonconforming, no-frontage parcel's house from 822 to 2,175 sq ft; HDC and Conservation Commission review; the ZBA hearing continued to October 3, 2023) is the fullest public record of the present neighborhood. The 2023 ZBA letter (PDF)

One discrepancy in the public filings themselves, noted without interpretation: the ZBA letter is signed "Matt Dawson and Chia Yun Sun," while a related filing email was sent under the name "Jessica Sun."

Epilogue

The Dawson years, 2015–present

Matthew Dawson and Chia-Yun (Jess) Sun bought 216 Pleasant Street in November 2015 from the Russell Family Trust, for $1,000,000; the deed was filed November 3, 2015 (Book 66331, Page 188).Confirmed

They first appear in the town's resident list of January 1, 2016 — a list that still also carries the Tarantellis at 216 that year, a co-listing that is a list artifact only: the Dawsons confirm firsthand that they never overlapped with the Tarantellis, whose occupancy was a Russell-era occupancy that ended with the November 2015 sale — and by the 2019 list they are the sole household at 216.Confirmed

Their tenure has been one of ongoing restoration of the 1854 house: a full window replacement project with 22 Marvin windows (2026), continued care of the Brine-era Inclinator elevator, and the 2026 deed-and-archive research project that produced this history.

Matt Dawson is the founder and director of the Spy Pond Adventure Club, an outdoor summer youth program on Spy Pond.

Reference

The neighbors

The houses carved from, or standing beside, the original Call estate — verified facts only, from the same deeds, censuses, and resident lists as the chapters above.

218 Pleasant Street — the carriage house

The original Call barn and carriage house, a dwelling from the 1920s. Florence V. Hunter lived there 1928–1949 (see Chapter 3). The Krook family held it from 1959 — Max Krook, and later Gulielma Krook alone, with a photographer in the household by 1987 — and Courtland Y. White was there from 1974. Today 218 is owned by Yu-Hsiou Liu; in 2026 a proposed addition to the house was before the Arlington Historic Districts Commission.

220 Pleasant Street

Joseph and Ethel Gray were at 220 in 1940. Howard S. Hibbett Jr., a teacher, and Akiko Y. Hibbett, a librarian, arrived by the resident list of January 1, 1961, from Boston. Akiko Y. Hibbett still owns 220 today, as trustee — a tenure of about 65 years.

214 Pleasant Street

A lot created by Harry Hunter's 1954 subdivision of the estate. It was sold on May 7, 1954 to Archie N. and Christine MacDonald (Book 8250, Page 305), and theirs is the first household the resident lists show there, in the list of January 1, 1956. The Costa family held 214 from 1974. Today it is owned by John James Garber III.

212 Pleasant Street

The second lot created by the 1954 subdivision. No household stands at 212 in the 1940 or 1950 census. The first named occupants are the Chorbajians: Elise Chorbajian in 1958, Arousyag Chorbajian in 1959, and Elise again through the 1970s–1990s; the 1997 Street Listing read for this history places Christina Kasica at 212. Today 212 is co-owned by Matt Dawson and John Garber and run as a short-term rental.

Chapter 6

Neighbors and the street

Pleasant Street runs along Spy Pond's western shore, and the pond — 103 acres, a kettle pond some 36 feet deep at its deepest, with two-acre Elizabeth Island — is the second main character in this house's story.

The layers, oldest first: Mother Batherick's capture of six redcoats near the pond on April 19, 1775. The mid-19th-century ice industry and the water company (1850). Camp Sheppard, the Civil War training camp near the pond. Streetcar-era suburbanization, then the 1920s boom — the town's population rose 93% in the decade the Hunters arrived. The last Spy Pond ice house is said to have burned in 1930, a date carried by low-authority sources; corroborate it in the Arlington Advocate before printing it. In 2010 the Arlington Land Trust, with Mass Audubon, ran a $250,000 campaign to buy Elizabeth Island for conservation. And there is the "Lizzie" legend — an alleged 1990 pet Komodo dragon released into the pond — explicitly a legend with no evidence, usable only as folklore. The present owners' 2023 letter is itself a primary source for 21st-century pond life: kayaking, skating, Town Day fireworks watched from the water, ice fishermen.

The street's other landmark stands a few doors up: the Prentiss-Payson House at 224–226 Pleasant, also listed on the National Register on April 18, 1985. For the estate's own houses — 212, 214, and 218 — the present-day occupants are documented from 2023 public filings (see Who's Who); their parallel histories across 1854–1950 are recoverable from the same directories, census districts, and assessor cards named throughout this history, and the 1930 (ED 9-169) and 1940 (ED 9-26) census pulls will capture the 212–220 households for those years as a by-product.

The pond side in the Boston directories, 1861–1870 — Birchard and the Gages at West Cambridge

Before the Arlington directories name the pond side street by street, the Boston directories already place its two central households in the town. The Boston Directory run for Charles Birchard and for the Gage ice family is now continuous 1861–1870 (page images read and archived).Confirmed In 1861 (printed p. 49) Birchard is “house at West Cambridge” as a partner in Birchard & Torrey, grocers, 183 State; in 1862 (printed p. 161) Addison Gage & Co. and Charles O. Gage, ice at 70 State, are both given a house at West Cambridge. In 1861, however, Charles O. Gage's personal entry still reads “h. at Charlestown” even though the firm's house is given as West Cambridge — he was still personally a Charlestown householder in 1861 and appears at West Cambridge from 1862.Confirmed Whether Birchard's West Cambridge house was today's 216 remains Inference — the Boston directories give no street or number. See Chapter 1 and ledger Item 49.

The pond side in 1869 — the directory

Six years before the Beers plate, the Somerville, Arlington and Belmont Directory for 1869–70 (Dudley & Greenough, 1869; Archive.org item arlingtoncitydir1869arli), read from its own pages, names the households on Pleasant Street near Spy Pond — without house numbers.Confirmed — from the directory itself On and around the estate stretch it lists: Charles Birchard, wholesale grocer (183 State, Boston), “house Pleasant, near Spy Pond” (p. 162), with Patrick Donnelly, “gardener, Charles Birchard's, Pleasant” (p. 168) — an estate with a resident gardener; Anna Gage, “widow Addison, house Pleasant, n. Spy Pond” (p. 170) — Addison Gage, who had assembled the estate parcels in 1852, was dead by 1869 — and Charles O. Gage, “ice dealer (128 State, B.), house Pleasant, near Spy Pond” (p. 170); Jackson H. Libby, “foreman of ice business for Addison, Gage & Co.” (p. 176) — the Gage ice business still running under Addison's name; and Charles Hill, George Hill, and Mary Hill, all on Pleasant near the pond (pp. 172–173). Just as telling is who is not there: the directory's Arlington C-section (pp. 164–166), read in full, contains no Corey or Cory entry and no Call entryNot found — verified negative — neither Henry Call nor E. W. Corey was an Arlington resident in 1869, which is what the Homer chain (Call → Birchard → Corey → Bartlett) predicts, with Corey arriving on the lot only by 1875 (below). That Birchard's house was specifically today's 216 remains Inference — the directory gives no numbers, and only the deeds settle it. See ledger Item 27.

The two Gages' endpoints are now fixed by the probate index. The Middlesex County Probate Index, Second Series 1870–1910, Vol. 1, read from the official index page images, lists Anna Gage of Arlington — Addison Gage's widow, who lived at the Pleasant Street house as his widow from 1869 onward — with her will probated in 1886 (case No. 20272), so she had died by 1886; and Charles O. Gage of Arlington — Addison's son, the pond-side ice dealer — with his will probated in 1892 (case No. 31715), so he had died by 1892.Confirmed — index-grade The index gives probate years and case numbers, not death dates; the will files themselves (Middlesex Probate Nos. 20272 and 31715) are the records that would give both, and the families. The same index carries a Charles Birchard of Framingham, will probated 1883 (case No. 15641) — recorded here as an unmerged candidate only: he may or may not be the Arlington grocer of Chapter 1, and he is not presented as the same man. And it carries a verified negative for the chain's first link: Henry Call appears nowhere in the Second Series (1870–1910), nor in the First Series (1648–1871) — no Middlesex probate was opened for him in either run.Not found — verified negative

The pond side in 1871–72 — Corey named, Birchard gone

Two years on, the Arlington Directory for 1871 & 2 (Greenough, Jones & Co., Boston, 1871; Archive.org item arlingtoncitydir1871arli) identifies the man the Beers plate would letter four years later. Printed p. 195: “Corey E. Willis, leather, (223 Congress, B.), h. Pleasant” — E. Willis Corey, a Boston leather dealer at 223 Congress Street, whose house was on Pleasant Street in Arlington.Confirmed The directory gives no more of his name: what the initial “E.” stands for is not stated, and expanding “E. Willis” to a full first name remains Unproven. The same directory's Arlington B section (printed pp. 192–194), read in full, has no entry at all for Charles Birchard — present at Pleasant near Spy Pond in 1869–70 — so the Birchard-to-Corey transition on Pleasant Street falls between the 1869–70 and 1871–72 directories.Confirmed See ledger Item 28.

The pond side in 1900 — the street renumbered

By 1900 the street carried numbers a modern reader recognizes. The Arlington and Belmont Directory for 1900 (Edward A. Jones, copyright 1900; Archive.org item arlingtoncitydir1900arli), in its Pleasant Street list (printed p. 172), places the Bartletts at 216 — Prof. & Mrs. George H. Bartlett, Edward H. Bartlett, and Miss Julia L. Bartlett — between 208 (Freeman N. Young; Frank E. Thompson) and 226 (Samuel G. Prentiss).Confirmed Pleasant Street was renumbered between the 1894 directory (the Bartletts at 88, Prentiss at 92) and 1900 (216 and 226): the same household, with the same neighbor beside it, at both numbers — so the directories themselves show that 88 Pleasant is today's 216. See Chapter 2 and ledger Item 29.

The pond side in 1875 — the Beers Atlas plate

F. W. Beers, County Atlas of Middlesex, Massachusetts (1875), Arlington village plate, printed pp. 103–104 (with the town plate p. 101), read from the Archive.org page images and archived in the project archive (maps-plans), is the earliest mapped census of who held the pond side of Pleasant Street.Confirmed — the plate itself North to south, the plate letters the pond-side holdings:

Hodgdon · Mrs. A. Gage · Capt. R. Hopkins · P. H. Peabody · S. B. Hinks · A. Griffith & Hewes · J. T. Trowbridge · Chas. Hill · C. W. Chamberlin · T. C. Bucknam · J. C. Weld · E. Gould · M. Morton · Chas. O. Gage · E. W. Corey · then Mrs. M. Payson / First Cong. Society / N. Pratt Est. · Mrs. Mayo · G. Hill.

The E. W. Corey lot ran from Pleasant Street to the Spy Pond shore and carried two buildings — one at the street, one mid-lot on a dashed drive. This confirms, from a primary source, that E. W. Corey held a pond-side Pleasant Street parcel in the 216 stretch in 1875 — the earlier “E. W. Corey” lead is now plate-confirmed. That the Corey lot is exactly today's 216 Pleasant Street remains Inference: house numbering and the 1954–56 Hunter subdivision intervened, and only the deeds settle the lot equivalence; the mid-lot building position is consistent with the house's set-back, elevated siting.

Observation, not a conclusion: the lot immediately south of Corey's was lettered “Mrs. M. Payson” — a Payson holding beside the Corey/Call parcel — while the Call family's own history includes an Emily Payson Call connection. No kinship is shown on the plate.

Russell's notes carry the estate's other houses further than the web research did, and the True Lists of 1952–1957, read directly in the follow-up passes, now confirm the 218 sequence for those years.Confirmed for 1952–57 218 — Bartlett's studio, then Florence Hunter's home — passed after her time to John E. and Madaline Marshall (in the January 1, 1951 list, newly arrived from Stow, and still there on January 1, 1952 — the 1950 list has no entry at 218 at all, and Russell's notes spell her Madeline and place them there in 1950); the January 1, 1953 list shows no listed residents at 218; then Robert H. and Patricia White (January 1, 1954 list, newly arrived from California, and still there on January 1, 1955 — Russell's notes place them a year early, in 1953), and Robert M. and Leona Weiss Brownell (January 1, 1956 and 1957 lists, newly arrived from Virginia — the notes place them a year early, in 1955; the same Brownells who bought lots E and F from the Hunters in 1956); G. Krook bought it from the Brownells in 1958, Max and Gulielma Krook held it in 1999, and in 2007 Gulielma's executrix, Katherine E. White, sold it to S. Plokhii. 220, sold off by Bartlett in 1918, was the Gray family's — Marcus J. and Ethel G. Gray — until 1955. And in the subdivision years the notes name Elise Chorbadjian at 212 (1956) and Archy H. and Christine Macdonald at 214 (1955–56), matching the 1954 MacDonald deed.

Arlington's population, 1850–2020 — the town the house grew old in

U.S. Census figures as compiled in the research. The 93% jump in the 1920s is the decade the Hunters arrived; the 1970 peak, 52,720, came and went during Helen Brine's tenure. No 1980–2010 values were in the source series, so none are drawn.

Appendix

Testing the six-owner chain

The chain, link by link — full evidence

The current owners' claim, from their 2023 ZBA letter: they are "only the sixth owners since it was built by Henry Call in 1854." The deed chain found in November 2026 supplies a sequence that matches the count exactly — Call (1) → Bartlett (2) → Hunter (3) → Brine (4) → Russell (5) → Dawson/Sun (6) — with no room for the "two intervening owners" once assumed between Bartlett and Russell. Rob Russell's own notes, received the same month, both strengthen and strain that sequence: they document the Bartlett estate's direct sale to Henry H. Hunter in 1923, and they put a seller named Hubbell between Call and Bartlett in 1886. Tested link by link:

LinkStatusEvidence / problem
Call → BartlettNot direct — Birchard and Corey intervene per the Homer manuscript (Birchard's 1869 residence confirmed by directory; house equivalence inference); Hubbell intervenes per Russell's notesRussell's notes: Gage sold lot A in 1854 (to a "Henry E. Cole"). The Homer manuscript's chain — Call → Charles Burchard → Corey → Bartlett — now has its middle link placed on the street by a primary source: the 1869–70 directory (p. 162) lists Charles Birchard (spelled Birchard, not Burchard), wholesale grocer, “house Pleasant, near Spy Pond,” with a resident gardener, Patrick Donnelly (p. 168) Confirmed; that his house was today's 216 is Inference (the directory gives no house numbers). The directory's C-section (pp. 164–166, read in full) has no Call and no Corey in 1869 Not found — verified negative, consistent with the chain. E. W. Corey in 1875 — his pond-side holding in the 216 stretch is confirmed by the 1875 Beers Atlas plate (exactly today's 216 remains inference; only the deeds settle the lot equivalence); and in 1886, per Russell's notes, John H. Hubbell sold land with the buildings A, B, C to George H. Bartlett. The six-owner count works at this link only if Birchard and Corey were tenants (or are overlooked) and Hubbell is overlooked, or held briefly as an intermediary — the notes themselves document Hubbell as a seller-owner. Bartlett's handwritten tenure in the notes runs from 1880, suggesting occupancy before the 1886 purchase. Settled by the Middlesex South grantor/grantee indexes (Call/Cole, Birchard/Burchard, Corey, Hubbell, Bartlett), 1854–1890.
Bartlett → HunterDirect sale documented in Russell's notes; deed not yet pulledRussell's notes: "George H. Bartlett estate (A) sold to Henry H. Hunter," 1923. Julia and Ethel remained listed at 216 into April 1924 — occupants after the sale, not owners. No deed into Hunter appears in the online registry index (his purchase predates reliable online indexing). If the notes are right, this link is direct; the deed itself, or the title recitals in the 1954 deed images, would prove it.
Hunter tenure, 1923–1956Confirmed as ownersBought from the Bartlett estate in 1923 (Russell's notes); proven independently by their own conveyances out — Harry and family held and sold the estate's lots in 1954–56, and tenants do not subdivide. List occupancy breaks for one year — the 1951 book has no 216 entry, refuting the notes for 1951 only — and resumes with Harry and Geraldine at 216 in the books of January 1, 1952, 1953, and 1954, confirming the notes for 1952–53 — and ends there: the 1955, 1956, and 1957 books contain no Hunter anywhere, so the household left during calendar 1954; title to 1954–56.
Hunter → Brine, June 30, 1954Confirmed as a sale; grantor in disputeBook 8280, Page 600 — the 216 house lot, to Helen S. Brine. The registry name index reads the grantors as Barry H. & M. Geraldine Hunter; Russell's notes say "Henry H. and Geraldine Hunter sold B (216) to Helen S. Brine." The deed image settles which Hunter granted. Brine is owner #4 either way.
Brine → Russell, June 8, 1981ConfirmedBook 14312, Page 236, $170,000, "Lot B." A same-day lien certificate names "Brine Helen S Est," suggesting her estate conveyed. Russell is owner #5.
Russell → Dawson/Sun, Nov. 3, 2015ConfirmedBook 66331, Page 188, $1,000,000; grantor Robert Mitchell Russell, trustee — which also confirms "Rob Russell" is Sharon's husband. Dawson/Sun are owner #6.

Verdict: the six-owner count is corroborated from 1923 forward, and strained at its first link. Every link from 1954 forward is proven by a recorded deed; the Bartlett→Hunter link is now documented by Russell's notes as a direct estate sale in 1923; and the resulting sequence — Call, Bartlett, Hunter, Brine, Russell, Dawson/Sun — is exactly six owners, matching the current owners' statement. But the notes themselves record John H. Hubbell selling the estate to Bartlett in 1886, with E. W. Corey in occupation in 1875, and the Homer manuscript — its middle link now corroborated by the 1869–70 directory, which places Charles Birchard on Pleasant Street near Spy Pond in 1869 — puts Birchard and Corey between Call and Bartlett as well: strictly counted, Hubbell is an owner the six-owner story skips, unless he held briefly as an intermediary and Birchard and Corey were tenants or intermediaries rather than counted owners. The honest formulation: six owners of the house as a residence since 1854, with one documented intermediary (Hubbell) in the title chain of the 1880s, and Birchard and Corey in occupation before him. The settling records: the Middlesex South grantor/grantee index books (in person, 208 Cambridge Street, Cambridge) and the title recitals in the 1954 deed images.

The Brine years · 1954–1981

Helen S. Brine — owner of 216 for 27 years, June 30, 1954 – June 8, 1981. Her biography beyond the lists is Not found — completion-pass web-index and FamilySearch SSDI searches returned 0 results, and no census or Mass. index entry was obtained; a 1981 lien certificate naming "Brine Helen S Est" suggests her estate conveyed the house. Appendix

The Russell notes

Rob Russell's estate research, in full: four typed pages headed "216, 218, 220 — Swan-Gage-Bartlett estate," with purple highlighter marks and a handwritten summary on the last page, received second-hand by the current owners in November 2026.

The notes are a year-by-year chronology of title and occupancy, apparently compiled from Middlesex deeds and the Arlington resident lists. In them the estate's parcels are lettered: A is the original estate (later split into A1, the 216 house lot, and A2, the 218 lot), and in 1953 the parcels were re-lettered B (216), C (214), D (212), E and F (218 and its lot); the notes also track 220, sold off by Bartlett in 1918. Entries without an address are about 216 unless a parcel letter says otherwise. Spellings below are as written, including the notes' internal inconsistencies — Cage for Gage, Chamberline for Chamberlin, "Hinter" for Hunter, Scammer for Scammell, Grey for Gray, and Howard Parker's middle initial given two ways. Ditto marks in the original are written out as "ditto." Bracketed remarks are this history's.

How the notes check against the registry

Where the notes and the MassLandRecords deed chain overlap, they agree: Helen S. Brine held 216 from 1954 to 1981 and sold to R. Russell (deeds Bk 8280/600 in, Bk 14312/236 out, $170,000); the Hunter subdivision of the mid-1950s, with the parcels re-lettered B–F in 1953; and the Brownell and Macdonald purchases (deeds 8652/134 and 8250/305). The notes also place Julia and Ethel Bartlett at 216 in 1921–1923, and Florence V. Hunter at 218 from 1930 through 1948 — the latter consistent with the books read directly (Florence at 218 in 1928, 1933, 1936, and 1949). But the November 2026 hard-evidence passes, which read the list books themselves, partly refute and partly confirm the notes on Geraldine: the notes put Geraldine M. Hunter in the 216 household in 1951–1953; the January 1, 1951 book has no entry for 216 at all and no Geraldine Hunter anywhere in the volume (the household is present on January 1, 1950 and gone on January 1, 1951) — yet the January 1, 1952 and January 1, 1953 books show Harry and Geraldine at 216 exactly as the notes say, and the 1954 book shows them there again. The same pass found two smaller divergences: for 1933 the book's text layer names MacLeod, Gladys X. (maid) and Stephens, Bertha J. at 216, where the notes give Nettie Richardson (and MacLeod a year earlier, initial I.); and the notes place the Marshalls at 218 in 1950, where the 1950 book has no entry at 218 and the 1951 book shows the Marshalls newly arrived from Stow. The follow-up read adds two more small divergences at 218: the books confirm the Marshalls there in 1952 and show no listed residents in 1953, where the notes already have the Whites — who appear in the book only in 1954, newly from California. The 1955–1957 read extends the pattern both ways: at 216 the books confirm the notes' Brine household — Frances S. and Helen S. Brine, Frost, and the Scammells in 1955 and 1956, with full names, ages, and occupations the notes never give — while at 218 the notes again run a year early, placing the Brownells there in 1955, where the book still shows the Whites; the Brownells appear in the books in 1956 and 1957, newly from Virginia. Points in open conflict, flagged where they occur in the chapters: Cole vs. Call for the 1854 buyer (the MHC form says Call; "Cole" has no documentary support so far); Henry vs. Barry as the 1954 grantor of lot B; the Henry legal-name claim (every record read says Harry H.); the notes' 1933 household against the book's text layer; and the six-owner count, which the notes' own 1886 Hubbell sale complicates. One trivial slip: the handwritten summary gives Brine "24 yrs" for 1954–1981, a span of 27 calendar years.

Reference

Era notes

Era notes — full text

A · Greek Revival in Massachusetts

The style dominated New England house-building c. 1830–1860: temple-front gables, heavy entablatures, pilasters, flushboard siding on formal facades. The NPS Arlington survey places 216 among the town's formal Greek Revival houses of the Pleasant Street area, distinguished by flush-board siding, in a town where Greek Revival farmhouses are otherwise common (the Symmes Jr. House, c. 1845; the Thomas Peirce House, c. 1830). The two-story, four-column pond-facing portico is the house's signature — a house designed to be seen from, and to look at, Spy Pond. (Nomination; NPS Arlington MRA text.)

B · The Spy Pond ice trade

Boston's ice trade began with Frederic Tudor's shipments from 1806, and Spy Pond was among the ponds harvested. Nathaniel Wyeth's 1825 horse-drawn ice cutter cut harvesting costs from about 30¢ to 10¢ a ton and losses from 66% to under 8%, industrializing the trade; the 1852 Gleason's print (Chapter: Prologue) shows Spy Pond harvesting with the railroad behind — the Fitchburg line made pond ice a Boston export. Ice houses (Gage's among them) and ice-tool manufacture clustered at the pond; the industry faded with mechanical refrigeration. If the current owners' documentary lead holds, Henry Call himself was an ice man — which would make the house a product of the trade it overlooked. (History Cambridge; 99% Invisible, "Frozen Assets.")

C · Lithography and art education in 19th-century Boston

Bartlett's career spans the trade's transformation: hand lithography in 1860s London, where he is credited with pioneering the steam press; pictorial "monumental" city maps; then the reproductive-process era documented in his own Pen and Ink Drawing (1903), whose 52 plates demonstrate drawing's "perfect adaptability to the modern processes of reproduction." Institutionally, the 1870 Massachusetts Drawing Act — the first such state mandate — created the demand, and the State Normal Art School (1873) supplied the teachers. Bartlett, its first instructor and principal 1883–1912, is arguably the most influential art-education administrator in Massachusetts history — and he commuted to it from this house for four decades. (School catalogs; 1917 Year Book; Geographicus.)

D · S. S. Pierce and the Boston grocery trade

From an 1831 Dock Square wholesale provisions firm supplying ship captains, S. S. Pierce became Boston's carriage-trade grocer — Copley Square (1887) and the Tudor clock-tower store at Coolidge Corner (1898–99) — famous for canned goods, wines, and delivery wagons and trucks serving Brookline and the suburbs. A general managership there (Harry Hunter, 1925) was a substantial white-collar post: the man at 216 ran one of the great food stores of greater Boston through the Depression. (Brookline Historical Society; company histories.)

E · Helen Keller's Massachusetts circle

Keller (1880–1968) was educated at Perkins School for the Blind in Watertown/South Boston and at Radcliffe; she worked for the American Foundation for the Blind from 1924 for 44 years and bequeathed her papers to it (now the Helen Keller Archive). Her household in these years included Anne Sullivan ("Teacher," d. 1936) and Polly Thomson, both named in the Hunter letters. The letters to Agatha are social, not institutional — thanks for sweets and gift baskets — placing the Hunters in Keller's personal gift-exchange circle in 1923–1932. What connected them is the open question; the archives named in Chapter 3 are where the answer, if any, survives.

F · 1920s home radio

Boston was an early radio city (WBZ from 1921; WNAC and WEEI followed), and a prosperous 1920s household installing a dedicated brass antenna/ground outlet — as at 216, c. 1928–1935 — was wiring the house for the new medium: an outside aerial, a ground connection, and a receiver in the parlor. The 1930 census asked every household whether it owned a "radio set"; the Hunter answer sits on the unpulled ED 9-169 schedule. By the mid-1930s a household like this one would have followed Boston-market network programming and news — and, for a Keller correspondent, a medium Keller herself famously championed for the blind.

G · Postwar subdivision of Arlington estates

Arlington's population peaked at 52,720 in 1970, and the postwar decades converted its remaining estates and farms to house lots. The 216 estate followed the pattern in 1954–56 — with a twist the deeds reveal: the subdivider was not an outside developer but the departing owner himself, Harry H. Hunter, selling the pond-side lots (212/214/218) to the MacDonalds and Brownells while his family sold the main house, on its reduced lot with a deeded pond easement, to Helen S. Brine. The town's 1985 National Register survey and the local Pleasant Street historic district later froze the result in place. The 2023 ZBA fight over 212 — a cottage on a no-frontage lot proposed to nearly triple in size — is the subdivision's still-unfolding consequence.

Verification ledger

Verification ledger — every item, in full

A verification pass set out to test this history's claims — including every claim taken from the second-hand Russell chronology — against the primary records themselves: census page images, resident-list page images, official indexes, and registry data, each with the citation a researcher would need to pull the same page again.

Two items were settled completely and decisively: the Arlington True Lists (Items 1–2, extended by the follow-up reads in Items 13–14), read in the books themselves on Internet Archive, and the MACRIS form (Item 8), read from the document itself. A later follow-up read (Item 16) has since settled Item 5 — the 1950 census margin address — from the page image itself, and further follow-up reads (Items 17–18) have since settled Item 4 — the 1940 census, Sheet 11A — and Item 9 — the PastPerfect record 2007.1.52. A verification run of November 21, 2026 (Items 21–22) has since read the National Register nomination file and both MACRIS records in full, settling the nomination's photograph count and what the state's inventory does — and does not — say about outbuildings and 218. The remaining items could not be settled to the hard-evidence standard in that pass — the census pages, draft cards, death index, PastPerfect record, and MassLandRecords index all live behind interactive search interfaces that could not be operated once the live research browser's budget was exhausted mid-mission. For each, the pass states exactly what was attempted, what locator information was established, and what remains open. Nothing in the "not read" rows is asserted beyond what the cited sources say. Evidence flags: [page image] = read from the scanned page; [book text layer] = read from the book's own OCR text layer on Internet Archive (the book itself, machine-read); [index] = web-index/search-result level only.

12 · Henry Call / Henry E. ColeComplete — entire 1850 West Cambridge schedule read; no entry (see Item 26)No entry for a Henry Call or a Henry E. Cole in West Cambridge was located in either the 1850 federal census or the 1855 Massachusetts census through the index searches available, and no Henry E. Cole of the right age surfaced in Charlestown. The MHC Form B's sole statement: first occupied by Henry Call, formerly of Charlestown — Call, no middle initial, no Cole anywhere in the form. A real Henry E. Call is attested nearby in user-contributed genealogy (WikiTree, citing FamilySearch): Henry Edwin Call, married his cousin Emily Payson Call (Charlestown family of Jonathan Call, 1786–1853) about 1849; the cited 1850 entry is Jonathan Call's Charlestown household and the 1860 entry shows Henry E. and Emily P. Call in Cambridge — locator context only, not proof he built 216 Pleasant, and it is Call, not Cole. Assessment: the "Cole" reading currently has no documentary support at all. Update — page-by-page read now complete (Item 26): the entire 1850 West Cambridge schedule (NARA reel M432-324, families 1–402, every page read from the page images) contains no Henry Call, no Henry E. Cole, no Burchard, no Corey, and no Gage Confirmed — from the record itself. Henry Call was therefore not living in West Cambridge in 1850, four years before he bought the estate in 1854; “formerly of Charlestown” remains the live lead. The one-man-or-two (Call vs. Cole) question itself remains unsettled — that still turns on the 1854 deed.

Beers, County Atlas of Middlesex, Massachusetts (1875), Arlington village plate, printed pp. 103–104 (with the town plate p. 101), read from the Archive.org page images; archived in the project archive (maps-plans). Confirmed (the plate itself): the pond side of Pleasant Street in 1875 was held, north to south, by Hodgdon, Mrs. A. Gage, Capt. R. Hopkins, P. H. Peabody, S. B. Hinks, A. Griffith & Hewes, J. T. Corey held a pond-side Pleasant Street parcel in the 216 stretch in 1875 — the earlier “E. W. Corey” lead is now plate-confirmed. Inference (labelled as such): that the Corey lot is exactly today's 216 Pleasant Street — house numbering and the 1954–56 Hunter subdivision intervened, and only the deeds settle the lot equivalence; the mid-lot building position is consistent with the house's set-back, elevated siting. Observation, not a conclusion: the lot immediately south of Corey's was lettered “Mrs. M. Payson,” a Payson holding beside the Corey/Call parcel, while the Call family's own history includes an Emily Payson Call connection — no kinship is shown on the plate.

Bartlett completion pass — summary of results (November 21–22, 2026)

Flags in that pass: [verified live] = read on the live page in the research browser; [index] = read via web-index/search-result text only.

  • Marriage (B2) — main positive result [verified live, FreeBMD], since updated: the completion pass found exactly two George Bartlett–Julia marriages, 1860–1870 — Bermondsey 1d 103, Jun 1862 (Julia Sherriff) and Barnet 3a 185, Dec 1866 (Julia Clark). A later live FreeBMD search (1855–1863) displaced both with a strong index-grade candidate: Newington 1d 347, Dec 1857 — George Hartnell Bartlett / Julia Louisa Smith (page-mates Ann Harvey, Elias Morton), fitting the censuses' marriage of about 1858. Maiden name Smith is therefore a strong candidate, not Confirmed — the GRO certificate for 1d 347 has not been obtained, and the index alone does not prove the pairing.
  • Russell dissertation (B7) — settled [verified live, MIT DSpace]: Uneasy welcome--the political economy in migration policy in Kuwait, Sharon Stanton Russell, PhD, MIT Political Science, 1987, advisor Myron Weiner. No abstract on the DSpace record; no ProQuest abstract retrieved.
  • MacJannet (B8) — partially settled [index, Tufts TARC MS024]: Vacation School of French established with Tufts College in 1944, “Located in Arlington, MA” — no street address in any Tufts source read. The residence question is since settled by the census margin (ledger Item 16): the MacJannets were at 208 Pleasant in 1950, Confirmed; a school at 216 or 218 is unproven / unsupported.
  • Carita B. Hunter (H5) — substantially identified [index, Simmons/Tufts]: Carita Hunter Lovejoy, Simmons '19, Mrs. Victor C. Lovejoy of Melrose by 1927, Tufts Shorthand and Typewriting instructor from 1929. Birth, marriage and death records not retrieved.
  • Not found, with searches documented in the chapters: Julia's death (B1, searched 1923–1935 — her death-or-removal window has since been narrowed to April 1924–April 1925 by the True Lists of 1924 and 1925, Item 56, though the death record itself remains not found); the Globe obituary (B3 — BPL database covers only 1932–1941 and 1953–2010); the remaining Bartlett children including “Po…” (B4 — Edward H. H. Bartlett, 1909 poll list, is an unproven candidate only); Ethel's death (B5 — Cambridge addresses 1930/1933 are the last traces read); Helen S. Brine and Frances S. Death: the True Lists now bracket it — Julia, 84, at 216 on April 1, 1924 (with Ethel, 56), and both gone by April 1, 1925, when the Hunter household is at 216 — so her death or removal falls in April 1924–April 1925 (ledger Item 56). Her Massachusetts death record itself is still not found: no Mass. death-index entry was retrieved from open indexes in the completion pass (searched 1923–1935), and no death date is stated. Her certificate (parents' names) remains a likeliest settler of her maiden name. Marriage: a live FreeBMD search (Bartlett, George, spouse first name Julia, 1855–1863) returned exactly two matches, the first a strong index-grade candidate — Newington, Dec 1857, vol. 1d, p. 347: George Hartnell Bartlett, on a page with Ann Harvey, Elias Morton, and Julia Louisa Smith, the page's only Julia — fitting the censuses' marriage of about 1858 (1900: married 42 years; 1910: married 52 years) and Newington's position adjoining Camberwell. The GRO index alone cannot pair groom and bride on a page (the other couple is Elias Morton / Ann Harvey), so the pairing and the maiden name Smith are Unproven — strong candidate, not Confirmed. Settling record: the GRO marriage certificate for Dec 1857, Newington, vol. 1d, p. 347 (not yet obtained), or the parish register entry, or a child's baptism naming the mother, or Julia's death certificate. The earlier candidates — Bermondsey 1d 103, Jun 1862 (Julia Sherriff) and Barnet 3a 185, Dec 1866 (Julia Clark) — are displaced by the 1857 entry, which predates them and carries George's full Hartnell name.
  10. The Boston Globe obituary of George H. Bartlett, March 1923. Full text not retrieved in the completion pass (Newspapers.com/ProQuest/Google snippets searched). The BPL Obituary Database indexes Globe/Herald/Transcript obituaries only for 1932–1941 and 1953–2010, so it structurally cannot supply a 1923 obituary. No survivors passage can be quoted.

Ave., Cambridge, Instructor of Watercolor (OCR-garbled — verify on page image); Harvard Crimson summer-school directory, July 12, 1933, at 1200 Mass. Ave., Cambridge. Whether she married, moved, or died in Arlington is unresolved.

Lovejoy, and her death record; no record read states her relationship to Florence V. Hunter in words.
  13. Florence V. Hunter, Thomas Forest, and Mary K. Dunleavy. Thomas Forest's Mass. death c. 1933–1937 not found, and no trace states his relationship, birthplace or occupation — the Agatha's-father hypothesis is unproven with no evidence for or against.   14. Barry Hunter's birth and Geraldine's marriage. Hunter to a Geraldine, 1949–1955, in any open index; the January 1, 1952 True List now gives her 1951 residence as Philadelphia, so Pennsylvania marriage records c. 1950–52 join the search.   15. The "Bartlett Homestead" photograph — settled: record read. Confirmed — closed The verification pass had searched the AHS PastPerfect portal, Digital Commonwealth, and DPLA by accession number (2007.1.52) and by title and surfaced no public record; the record has since been read directly (ledger Item 18). PastPerfect record 2007.1.52 is titled “Big Book p.52” (1920–1942, 8 images); its image 8 is captioned “Bartlett Homestead, 216 Pleasant St” and shows the house from the street — white two-story clapboard, two chimneys, trees, a utility pole, and a 1940s car in front. The image is CC BY-NC-ND, with rights status not evaluated. Retained here as a closed item so the settlement is on the record.
  16. Barry H. and M. Geraldine Hunter — who were they? Their kinship to Harry is still open (Geraldine's residence at 216 is now confirmed for 1952–54 by the list books themselves — only the notes' 1951 placement is refuted — and the 1952 list gives her 1951 residence as Philadelphia). Harry H. Hunter's Middlesex probate file (heirs-at-law), the Massachusetts marriage index c. 1950–54 (a Hunter remarriage), Barry's birth record, and the recitals in the deed images at Book 8250/305 and 8280/600. Settles their kinship to Harry — and Barry's birth record may name Agatha's maiden name.
  17. Harry H. Hunter's death — after February 14, 1956. The Massachusetts death index 1956–1970, his Middlesex probate file, and Mount Pleasant Cemetery. His origins route runs through his September 1918 draft card, the St. Albans border lists, his naturalization petition (NARA Boston), and the 1901/1911 Canadian censuses.
  18. Helen S. Brine's life, and the house's occupants 1986–1995. Her Middlesex South Probate file (c. 1981) and the Massachusetts death index c. 1980–81 remain the settling records for her life; the Arlington True Lists and directories for everyone who lived at 216 are now read continuously through January 1, 1985 (ledger Items 13–14, 39, 42, 43, 44, 45, 46, 47, and 48): the Hunters held 216 through January 1, 1954, and the Brine–Frost–Scammell household is documented for 1955–1981 — Brine, Frost, and Madeleine Scammell throughout 1969–1975, with Clara H. Currier (from Boston) and Keith A. Larson (from Cambridge) joining in 1974–75, the same five still at 216 on January 1, 1978 and January 1, 1979, four of them on January 1, 1980, Frances M. Frost by then gone, and just two — Brine (90, Retired) and Larson (39) — on January 1, 1981, Clara H. Currier and Madeleine Scammell by then gone. Her departure falls between January 1, 1981 and the June 8, 1981 deed to the Russells, and the January 1, 1982 list closes the run: Brine gone, Robert Mitchell Russell (40, Physician) and Sharon Stanton Russell (37) in place, Larson (40) stayed on — no True List year for the Brine era remains unread. The January 1, 1983 list (printed p. 94, Precinct 8; ledger Item 46) carries the Russell household a year on: Robert Mitchell Russell (41, Physician), Sharon Stanton Russell (38, Planner), Larson (41, Edit/Res) still staying on, and a new resident, Gettner Shormeen (20, Student; relationship unstated). The January 1, 1984 list (printed p. 90, Precinct 8; ledger Item 47) holds the household at three — Larson (42, Edit/Res), Robert Mitchell Russell (42, Physician; the book misprints his surname as “Fussell”), and Sharon Stanton Russell (39, Planner) — with Shormeen gone. The January 1, 1985 list (printed p. 90, Precinct 8; ledger Item 48) carries the household a year on — Robert Mitchell Russell (43, Physician), Sharon Stanton Russell (40, Planner), Larson (43) now printed as Student against Edit/Res in 1975–1984, and Gettner Sharmeen (Student; no age printed) back after her 1984 absence, her name spelled “Sharmeen” in 1985 against “Shormeen” in 1983. The 1993 list (ledger Item 50) has since been read ahead of the intervening years: the same four residents continue at 216 — Keith A. Larson (51, Editor), Brooke Alden Russell (22, Staff Assistant; previously listed as “C Student”), Robert Mitchell Russell (51, Physician), and Sharon Stanton Russell (48, Planner) — their ages advancing two years from the 1991 list, the 1992 list having repeated the 1991 ages unchanged, and the household printed only in the book's Precinct 6 section against its own Street Index, an anomaly flagged, not harmonized. The 1997 list (the “1997 Street Listing,” printing year of birth instead of age; ledger Item 51) has since been read ahead of the intervening years as well: only three residents remain at 216 — Keith A. Larson (b. 1941, Editor), Robert Mitchell Russell (b. 1941, Physician), and Sharon Stanton Russell (b. 1944, Planner) — and Brooke Alden Russell, at 216 in the lists from 1988 through 1996, is gone and appears nowhere in the book. The 1999 list (the “1999 Street Listing,” printing year of birth instead of age; ledger Item 52) has since been read as well: the same three remain at 216 — Keith A. Larson (b. 1941, occupation now printed “Edit Dept”), Robert Mitchell Russell (b. 1941, Physician), and Sharon Stanton Russell (b. 1944, Planner) — and there is no resident change at any estate address between the 1998 and 1999 lists (Kasica at 212, Costa at 214, Krook at 218, Hibbetts at 220, Glaubers at 221; 208 has no entry). The 2000 list (the “2000 Street Listing”; ledger Item 53) has since been read as well: the same three remain at 216 on January 1, 2000 — Keith A. Larson (b. 1941, Editor), Robert Mitchell Russell (b. 1941, Physician), and Sharon Stanton Russell (b. 1944, Planner) — with no resident change at 216 between the 1999 and 2000 lists. What remains open under this item is the Russell era, 1986–1992 and 1994–1996. One list figure is flagged, not harmonized: the 1970 list prints Brine's age as 71, against 78 in 1969 and 80 in 1971.
  19. Where did Harry and Geraldine Hunter go after 1954? Unproven / open The True Lists place them at 216 on January 1, 1954 and nowhere in Arlington in 1955, 1956, or 1957 — they left during calendar 1954. Harry was alive on February 14, 1956 (deed, Book 8670/81). No record read places either of them anywhere after 216. Settling records: Harry's Middlesex probate file and Massachusetts death record (post-1956), Geraldine's Philadelphia connections (her 1951 residence), and the 1955–57 directories of wherever they landed.
  20. Did Frances S. Brine die in 1956? Unproven / open She is at 216 on January 1, 1955 (89, retired) and January 1, 1956, and absent on January 1, 1957. Disappearance from the list is consistent with death at about 90 but does not prove it — she may equally have moved or entered care. Settling records: the Massachusetts death index 1956 (and 1955–57) under Frances S. Brine, and Mount Pleasant Cemetery.

The MacJannets' home is now settled: 208 Pleasant, confirmed by the 1950 census margin (ED 9-38, sheet 4; ledger Item 16) and the 1949–1951 True Lists. Any claim that the school was at 216 or 218 Pleasant is Unproven / unsupported by the census and the town lists. What remains open is only the school's own address and years, if it differed from the home. No independent record was read in that pass: web-index searches and FamilySearch SSDI searches (Helen Brine, death 1980–1982, Mass.; and all years) returned 0 results, and no census schedule, Mass. index entry, or maiden name was obtained for either woman. The follow-up read of the 1955–1957 True Lists has since supplied the first record of both: Helen at 216, 64, "personnel," in 1955 and 66, retired, in 1957; Frances at 216, 89, retired, in 1955–56 and gone by 1957 (her possible 1956 death is the open item above). Their relationship to each other, if any, is stated in no record read.
  24. The pre-1954 deed links. Call→Bartlett (through Birchard and Corey, per the Homer manuscript — Birchard's 1869 Pleasant Street residence is now directory-confirmed, ledger Item 27, though his house's equivalence to 216 is inference) and Bartlett→Hunter remain unproven on the deeds: the Middlesex South grantor/grantee index books, in person at 208 Cambridge Street, Cambridge (pre-1974 deed images are not online), plus the title recitals in the 1954 deed images on MassLandRecords.
  25. Is the 1875 Corey lot exactly today's 216? Inference — open The Beers Atlas plate (1875, village plate pp. 103–104) confirms E. W. Corey held a pond-side Pleasant Street parcel in the 216 stretch in 1875, running to the Spy Pond shore with two buildings (one at the street, one mid-lot on a dashed drive). That the lot is exactly today's 216 is inference only: house numbering and the 1954–56 Hunter subdivision intervened, and only the deeds settle the lot equivalence. The mid-lot building position is consistent with the house's set-back, elevated siting. The 1869–70 directory brackets his arrival from below: its Arlington C-section (pp. 164–166, read in full) has no Corey or Cory entry Not found — verified negative — Corey was not an Arlington resident in 1869, and appears as the lot's holder only by 1875 (ledger Item 27). Settling records: the Middlesex South grantor/grantee indexes and deeds under Call, Corey, and Hubbell, c. 1854–1890, read against the plate. Observation only, not a conclusion: the lot immediately south of Corey's was lettered “Mrs. M. Payson,” while the Call family history includes an Emily Payson Call connection — no kinship is shown on the plate.
  26. Was Birchard's 1869 house the Call house — and who was Sarah Ann Burchard/Birchard? House equivalence: Inference Sarah Ann: Unproven / open The 1869–70 directory (p. 162) places Charles Birchard — spelled Birchard, not the Homer manuscript's “Burchard” — on Pleasant Street near Spy Pond in 1869, with a resident gardener, Patrick Donnelly (p. 168) Confirmed. The Boston Directory run now places him at West Cambridge continuously 1861–1870 — in 1861 (printed p. 49) “house at West Cambridge” as a partner in Birchard & Torrey, grocers, 183 State Confirmed (ledger Item 49) — but those directories likewise give no street or house number, so that his West Cambridge house was the Call house (today's 216) remains inference from the Homer chain and the 1875 Beers plate, not proof, and is not upgraded to Confirmed; the Call→Birchard and Birchard→Corey deeds settle it. Sarah Ann Burchard, the 1857 Gage lessee in Russell's notes, may be recorded under the spelling “Birchard”; searches under both spellings have so far found no matching person, and her identity — including any kinship to Charles — remains open. Settling records: the Middlesex South deeds and the 1857 lease instrument itself, read under both spellings. See ledger Item 27.
  27. Keller–Hunter correspondence in the archives. Partly searched: the Perkins Archives' Keller ephemera collection (AG160) lists no Hunter item in its correspondence container list, and no RR Auction lot names a consignor. Still to run: the AFB Helen Keller Archive's internal search for "Agatha Hunter," a direct Perkins archivist query, and the Helen Keller Papers at the Schlesinger Library. Settles: whether the correspondence survives institutionally, and how Agatha and Keller met.
  28. Henry Call — and which Hill sold to him? The MHC Form B names him — Call, not Cole — and the verification pass found no documentary support for any Henry (E.) Cole connected to this house; a Charlestown-area Henry Edwin Call is attested in genealogy sources as locator context only. The Homer manuscript says Call bought in 1854 from “Mr. Hill.” The 1850 Census is now read in full for West Cambridge (entire schedule, families 1–402, every page read from the page images, NARA reel M432-324): it contains no Henry Call, no Henry E. Cole, no Burchard, no Corey, and no Gage Confirmed — from the record itself, so Call was not living in West Cambridge in 1850 and “formerly of Charlestown” remains the live lead. The Hills are there in force, and the census supplies three candidates in consecutive West Cambridge households on written p. 332 (image n320): Amos Hill, 76, $8,000 in real estate; Amos Hill Jr., 40, farmer, $12,500; Henry W. Hill, 38, farmer, $12,800 Confirmed census facts — neighboring farmers with $8,000–$12,800 in real estate, each an Unproven candidate, since no record yet says which Hill sold. A second negative now brackets him from the other side: the 1869–70 directory's Arlington C-section (pp. 164–166, read in full) contains no Call entry Not found — verified negative — Call was not an Arlington resident in 1869 either, consistent with the Homer chain's account that he had sold to Birchard and left (ledger Item 27). Still open: Charlestown directories; West Cambridge censuses 1860–80 and the 1855 reading (the 1850 West Cambridge reading above is now complete); the unidentified ice documentary named in the 2023 ZBA letter; and above all the Middlesex South grantor index and the 1854 deed itself for his land purchase (seller, price, acreage).

She left Tufts without graduating Confirmed. Still open: her birth record, her marriage, and her later life — Not found, still being researched; Tufts alumni / Jackson College records for Joan Hunter of 216 Pleasant Street (Arlington High School Class of 1941; Jackson College Class of 1945 per the 1942 Jumbo directory) remain a named next source. Retained here as a partly closed item so the settlement is on the record.

This history was compiled in November 2026 from the records and sources above. Two standing cautions run through it. First, the Hunters of 216 Pleasant are never merged with the unrelated Harry Hunter of 62 Amsden Street, Arlington (wife Josephine V.), or with any other same-name person — a web search for a Harry H. Hunter obituary in November 2026 returned only unrelated men. Second, machine transcriptions — census name indexes and town-list OCR alike — are treated as fallible throughout: on the 1950 schedule, the National Archives' own AI index reads this house's Harry as "Hunter Harris H," and only the page image gives his name right. Living people are covered from public records and published sources only.
